t: How would you debug sustained high CPU in a Java service, and what are the common causes
k: debug high proving threads methods burning metrics separation async profiler proven cause usually tight loop expensive serialization lock contention regex backtracking pressure evidence collect instance separate application sampling produce flame graph touching split large fraction garbage collection heap filling repeatedly allocation business logic samples thread stacks frequency names hottest widest bars removing guesswork common causes loops algorithms json showing spinning pathological excessive short-lived distinct fingerprint specific scaling without diagnosis multiplies defect across machines imagine teller national bank india sweating working
kp: always collect evidence with cpu metrics, thread dumps, and a sampling profiler before changing any code. the first split is application cpu versus garbage-collection cpu because their fixes are opposite. an async or sampling profiler produces a flame graph that names the hottest methods directly. common causes are tight loops, expensive serialization, lock contention, regex backtracking, and gc pressure. each cause has a distinct fingerprint in the flame graph or thread dump that guides the fix. never scale out a cpu-bound service before proving the root cause, because scaling a defect just burns more money. high cpu and high latency are different problems: a slow service with idle cpu is waiting, not computing.

t: Thousands of threads are suddenly created and CPU spikes: why is "add more servers" wrong, and how do you investigate

kp: adding servers multiplies a thread defect across more machines instead of fixing it, raising cost without solving the root cause. thread dumps reveal what thousands of threads are actually doing: waiting on a slow dependency or runnable in hot code. thread names are a decisive clue: ever-incrementing pool names or raw thread-n names reveal unbounded creation. the two root causes are unbounded thread spawning per request and a badly sized pool blocked on a slow dependency. cpu spikes from thread explosions are mostly context-switching overhead, not useful computation. the fix is a single bounded thread pool sized to the downstream dependency, with a bounded queue and fail-fast rejection. for io-bound workloads, consider virtual threads or reactive non-blocking io, but always bound the real resource: the dependency.

kp: decompose into focused microservices: user/auth, location, trip, matching, pricing, payment, notification, and ratings. real-time location is the defining challenge: drivers send gps every few seconds into an in-memory geo-index partitioned by region. the matching engine reads from the in-memory geo-store and claims drivers atomically to prevent double assignment. database-per-service lets the location service use a fast geo-store while payment uses a strongly consistent relational db. communication is a deliberate mix: synchronous for immediate answers and asynchronous kafka events for high-volume flows. payment uses the outbox pattern and idempotency keys so retries never double-charge the rider. scale horizontally and partition everything geographically so load and failures stay local.

kp: the system is write-rarely and read-constantly, so optimize the redirect path to be cache-first and sub-millisecond. counter plus base62 guarantees collision-free short codes by construction; hashing requires collision detection and retry. range allocation gives each server a block of counter values so codes are minted locally without a central bottleneck. http 301 is permanent and lets browsers cache it, losing analytics; 302 is temporary and sends every click to your server. custom aliases go through the same uniqueness constraint and are validated against a reserved-word list. analytics are recorded off the hot redirect path by emitting click events to kafka for async aggregation. base62 with 7 characters gives trillions of codes; size the length to exceed projected volume with headroom.

kp: no single acid transaction spans services; the accepted pattern is a saga of local transactions with compensating undo steps. transaction boundaries live inside each service, never across them; the outbox pattern makes state and events atomic. create the order synchronously for an immediate order id, then drive payment and inventory through kafka as a saga. if inventory succeeds but payment fails, the saga runs the inventory compensation to release the reserved stock. idempotency keys ensure retries never create duplicate orders or double-charge the customer. prefer orchestration over choreography for the money path because explicit, auditable control matters. monitor saga state with metrics for started, completed, compensated, and stuck sagas, with a dead-letter queue for poison events.

k: guarantee loss double-debit per-partner bulkhead circuit breaker fail fast transaction-id idempotency replays stored result saga compensations plus reconciliation external banks rest endpoints resources banking partners expose messaging apis transactional cannot enroll two-phase commit even blocking locks catastrophic payments partner gets queue dedicated consumer down backlog starve healthy ones counts recent failures opens stopping threads piling dead endpoint carries transaction instead debiting again money moves compensating reversals periodic compares ledgers resolve divergence imagine rajesh sends national bank india must pass three
kp: two-phase commit is wrong because external partners are rest endpoints, not xa resources, and blocking locks are catastrophic for payments. a per-partner bulkhead (queue + dedicated consumer) ensures one down partner cannot block the others. a circuit breaker per partner detects failure early and fails fast instead of piling up stuck calls. transaction-id idempotency ensures replays after recovery return the stored result, never double-debiting. a saga with compensating transactions (refund, reverse) provides eventual consistency without distributed locking. money is held in a durable in-flight escrow tied to the transaction id so it is always accounted for. periodic reconciliation compares ledgers with each partner by transaction id to resolve any divergence.

t: How would you model a double-entry ledger in a relational database with DB-level correctness
k: double-entry ledger records event immutable append-only entries zero enforced database constraints balances derived summing corrections made reversing money moved books never silently wrong conservation financial produces whose signed amounts exactly ever transferred accounts created destroyed immutability posted entry permanent historical fact transactions updates deletes db-level enforcement deferred constraint trigger rejects commit regardless attempted idempotency unique business table prevents duplicate postings retries account balance mutable column drift think national bank india accountant giant book written moves writes least lines must cancel
kp: every financial event is two or more entries whose signed amounts sum to exactly zero: money is moved, never created or destroyed. entries are append-only and immutable; corrections are new reversing transactions, never updates or deletes. a deferred constraint trigger at commit time rejects any transaction whose entries do not net to zero. not-null on account, amount, and currency prevents malformed entries; a non-zero check rejects meaningless zero entries. a unique business key on the transaction prevents duplicate postings from retries. balances are derived by summing immutable entries, not stored as a mutable column that can drift. periodic snapshots are a rebuildable performance cache, never the source of truth.

t: How would you design a tamper-evident audit log
k: tamper-evident audit chains record hash previous edit deletion breaks chain backed worm storage periodic signed checkpoints tiered cold index append-only enough plain table controls change compromised account still alter rows looks normal afterward stores content previous_hash depends entire history single later links snapshots head catch whole-chain rewrites attacker cannot forge signature write-once-read-many prevents tampering detects prevention detection needed recent stays fast queryable store moves cheap searchability imagine national bank india keeps logbook page corner seal made melting together current text
kp: a plain append-only table is not tamper-evident because a privileged user can still alter rows silently. each record stores hash(content + previous_hash), so changing any record breaks the chain and all later links. periodic signed checkpoints of the chain head catch whole-chain rewrites because the attacker cannot forge the signature. worm (write-once-read-many) storage prevents tampering; the hash chain detects it: both prevention and detection are needed. tier by age: recent data in a fast queryable store, old data in cheap cold storage with an index. the hash chain spans tiers because each record carries its previous hash regardless of where it is stored. include a sequence number and timestamp in the hashed content so reordering is also detectable.

kp: the key fix is making the resend button re-send the existing valid otp instead of generating a new one, killing retry-storm amplification. multi-level rate limiting (per-user, per-ip, per-provider, global) protects at different scopes. a ttl-and-priority queue smooths the burst to the provider's sustainable rate, discarding expired otps automatically. multi-provider failover with a token bucket per provider routes to a provider that still has capacity. totp (time-based one-time password) needs no sms and adds zero provider load, making it the strategic long-term fallback. store otps in redis with expiry as ttl so the resend check is a cheap key lookup. the through-line is: reduce provider calls first, then pace what remains, then fall back to channels that need no provider.

kp: physical isolation by priority: separate kafka topics with dedicated consumer groups for critical and bulk messages. a shared queue causes starvation because millions of marketing messages sit ahead of the next otp in arrival order. dedicated consumer groups give independent offsets, independent lag, and independent scaling. provider capacity must also be isolated: a shared rate limit still starves the critical path at the final hop. a single priority queue is weaker because it shares consumers, provider rate, and failure modes. the bulk pipeline can be paused during incidents while the critical pipeline keeps delivering. classify each notification at the edge so marketing can never accidentally enter the critical topic.

t: How would you design a real-time chat / messaging system like WhatsApp or Slack
k: persist deliver websockets live full-duplex delivery redis pub-sub fan-out across servers order conversation sequence number fall back queue plus push offline users write message durable storage assign acknowledging sender delivering anyone persistent channel server client send frames without re-establishing monotonic counter assigns clients render arrival receipts reached device read user opened separate states recipient already persisted enqueue notification replay reconnect scaling sticky sessions lets arriving reach socket national bank india secure messaging rajesh sends relationship manager priya writes permanent ledger
kp: persist first, deliver second: the database is the source of truth, and delivery is a projection of what is already stored. websockets provide full-duplex persistent connections for instant bidirectional message delivery. per-conversation ordering uses a monotonic sequence number assigned at persist time, not global ordering. delivery and read are two distinct state transitions tracked per recipient per message. offline users receive a push notification; on reconnect the client replays from its last-seen sequence. scaling stateful websocket servers uses sticky sessions plus redis pub-sub fan-out across servers. deduplicate with a client-generated message id so retries never create duplicate messages.

kp: space-based architecture keeps hot data in a replicated in-memory grid so requests hit memory instead of a database. each processing unit holds business logic and a slice of the data, serving reads and writes from ram. a separate data-writer process flushes changes to the backing database asynchronously, off the critical path. scaling works by adding processing units, each bringing its own memory and cpu, giving roughly linear throughput growth. it is justified only when the database is the proven bottleneck under extreme bursty load such as trading, flash sales, or ticketing. trade-offs include eventual consistency between the grid and the database, durability risk if replicas fail before a flush, and high operational complexity. simpler options like caching, read replicas, and sharding should be exhausted before reaching for this architecture.

kp: refresh-ahead proactively reloads a hot value in the background before its ttl expires, so readers never hit a slow miss. caffeine implements this with refreshafterwrite, which returns the stale value immediately while one background thread reloads. a cache stampede (thundering herd) happens when many keys expire at the same instant and a flood of readers all reload simultaneously. probabilistic early recompute (xfetch) makes each read refresh with a probability that grows as expiry nears, scattering refreshes over a window. per-key ttl jitter is the cheapest defense: keys loaded together get slightly different ttls so they do not expire at once. single-flight (one-loader) ensures at most one reload per key, complementing the time-spreading of probabilistic recompute. refresh-ahead only warms keys that are actually read, which is correct because there is no point refreshing something nobody wants.

kp: the error rate metric measures the fraction of requests returning an error; reliability measures sustained ability to produce correct outcomes. retries can keep the error rate low by doing amplified hidden downstream work, but the hidden work is itself the bottleneck. removing retries raises the visible error rate because failures are no longer masked by eventual success. three good things happen: downstream load drops (one call per request), capacity is preserved for the majority, and the dependency recovers faster. this is not an argument against all retries, but against retries as a reflex and against measuring health by a single surface metric. the right long-term design is retries governed by a budget and circuit breaker, plus explicit load shedding. also measure the amplification factor (downstream calls per client request) and dependency saturation, not just the surface error rate.

kp: availability measures 'did it respond'; reliability measures 'was the response correct over time.' a service returning http 200 while producing incorrect financial state scores perfect availability but is deeply unreliable. silent incorrectness is worse than an outage: it accumulates undetected and requires painful reconciliation. slis must measure business correctness: 'fraction of transfers that actually settled with correct balances,' not just 'fraction returning 200.' correctness slis require instrumenting the actual outcome: reconciliation, synthetic end-to-end transactions, and intended-vs-actual comparison. for financial systems, reliability dominates availability: a bank would rather fail a transfer honestly than complete it incorrectly. a system optimizing only its availability number by swallowing errors is optimizing the wrong metric.

kp: one primary (master) takes all writes and replicates to replicas (slaves) that serve reads. replication can be async (fast but risk of data loss) or sync (safe but adds write latency). a dead replica just loses read capacity with no data loss; reads shift to other replicas. a dead primary halts writes until a replica is promoted, risking loss of not-yet-replicated writes. split-brain is the danger: two nodes both think they are primary and accept conflicting writes. replication lag creates eventual consistency on reads; route fresh reads to the primary. primary-replica scales reads but not writes; for write scalability, you need sharding.

kp: a topic is a named, logical category of events such as `transfers` or `transactions` that holds all records of a particular type. a partition is an ordered, append-only, immutable log within a topic that is the unit of parallelism and ordering. an offset is a monotonically increasing 64-bit integer that uniquely identifies a record's position within a specific partition. a record is located by the triple of topic, partition, and offset. the record's partition is chosen by hashing its key, so the same key always lands in the same partition and stays ordered. consumers track progress by committing offsets to the internal `__consumer_offsets` topic. offsets enable replay: a consumer can seek to any offset to re-read historical data.

kp: topic proliferation is the kafka problem where routing dimensions multiply the number of flat topics that must be created and managed. each kafka topic requires explicit creation, partition sizing, replication, retention settings, acls, and monitoring. a cluster has a practical ceiling on total partitions because each consumes broker memory, file handles, and controller metadata. adding a new routing dimension (country, type, size) multiplies the topic count combinatorially. solace avoids proliferation because topics are publish-time strings in one hierarchical namespace, not pre-created objects. in solace, adding a new routing need is a new subscription pattern, not a new broker object. the practical answer is often to let solace route live events and let kafka store durably, rather than forcing kafka to route finely.

kp: each partition has one leader replica that handles all reads and writes, and one or more follower replicas that passively copy data from the leader. the isr (in-sync replica set) is the leader plus all followers caught up within `replica.lag.time.max.ms`, and only isr members can be elected leader. with `acks=all`, the leader acknowledges a write only after every isr member has copied it, providing the strongest durability guarantee. `min.insync.replicas` sets the floor: if the isr shrinks below this number, the leader rejects writes rather than risk data loss. unclean leader election (`unclean.leader.election.enable=true`) promotes an out-of-sync replica and risks data loss; it is disabled in banking systems. monitoring isr-shrink events is critical because a chronically shrinking isr signals an unhealthy broker that threatens durability.

kp: at-most-once: each message is delivered zero or one time, so messages may be lost but never duplicated (commit offset before processing). at-least-once: each message is delivered one or more times, so messages are never lost but may be duplicated (process then commit offset). exactly-once: each message is effectively processed once, with neither loss nor duplication (idempotent producer + transactions). the delivery semantic is determined by when the consumer commits its offset relative to processing and the producer's acks and idempotence settings. for most banking use cases, at-least-once with an idempotent consumer is the pragmatic and robust choice. true exactly-once is native only to kafka-to-kafka flows; external side effects need application-level idempotency.

kp: a partition is a directory of segment triples: .log (data), .index (offset index), .timeindex (time index). only the active (newest) segment is written to; closed segments are immutable. the offset index is a sparse map from logical offset to byte position for fast lookups via binary search. segments roll when they hit segment.bytes or segment.ms, whichever comes first. delete retention removes whole closed segments; compaction rewrites closed segments to latest-per-key. the active segment is never eligible for retention or compaction. segment size is a trade-off: smaller gives finer cleanup but more file-handle and index overhead.

kp: a dead letter topic (dlt) stores messages that fail processing after all retries are exhausted, so they can be inspected and replayed later. spring kafka provides `@retryabletopic` with automatic retry topics and a `@dlthandler` for final failure handling. a poison pill is a message that always fails no matter how many times you retry it, and the dlt is the safe destination for such messages. `defaulterrorhandler` with `deadletterpublishingrecoverer` is the programmatic alternative to annotation-driven retry and dlt. retries use exponential backoff to avoid hammering a failing downstream system, while the dlt captures the message after backoff is exhausted. monitoring dlt depth and alerting on new arrivals is critical in production banking systems to catch silent processing failures. consumer idempotency combined with dlt ensures that no transaction is lost and no transaction is applied twice.

k: poison pill blocks partition forever record never succeed bounded retries route dead letter topic commit past keep flowing poison-pill message consumer successfully process causing retry fail blocking indefinitely separate failed records published error metadata inspected triaged replayed offline configured maximum number attempts routed prevents infinite loops defaulterrorhandler spring kafka handler catches processing exceptions routes unrecoverable deadletterpublishingrecoverer recoverer publishes original headers exception classification separating transient failures worth retrying permanent straight imagine national bank india settlement clerk stack transfer slips slip garbage
kp: a poison pill is a record the consumer can never process, causing an infinite retry loop that blocks the whole partition. kafka processes records in offset order and only commits after success, so one failing record stalls everything behind it. the standard fix is a dead letter topic: after bounded retries, publish the record plus error metadata to a dlt and commit past it. in spring kafka, use defaulterrorhandler with deadletterpublishingrecoverer and a configurable backoff. classify exceptions: transient failures (database timeout) are retried; permanent failures (validation error) go straight to dlt. deserialization poison pills need a safe deserializer (errorhandlingdeserializer) to avoid crashing before the error handler runs. the dlt must be monitored and owned, or it becomes a silent graveyard.

kp: a dlq only isolates failures -- it does not fix, alert, or process anything by itself. without monitoring, a dlq converts a loud failure (stuck partition) into a silent one (growing pile nobody sees). monitoring must alert on dlq depth and growth rate, and page the owning team, not just appear on a dashboard. root-cause classification separates transient failures (replay after recovery) from permanent failures (fix or discard). a written and tested replay/redrive procedure avoids improvising under pressure during an incident. clear ownership with a service-level agreement for draining the dlq prevents shared responsibility becoming nobody's responsibility. treat a dlq as an incident-response mechanism: alerts, runbooks, triage, ownership, and metrics.

t: Choosing between Kafka, AWS SQS, and RabbitMQ for asynchronous communication

kp: kafka is a durable, replayable event log where many independent consumer groups read the same events at their own pace. aws sqs is a fully managed cloud queue designed for simple point-to-point job distribution with zero infrastructure to operate. rabbitmq is a smart broker with exchanges, routing keys, and bindings that give fine-grained control over message routing. the mental model is: kafka records that something happened, sqs says a job needs doing, rabbitmq decides where to route this message. a mature banking platform often uses all three: kafka for the event backbone, sqs for cloud-native background jobs, rabbitmq for routing-heavy integrations. kafka retains messages for replay regardless of consumption; sqs deletes messages after acknowledgment; rabbitmq routes and delivers once.

kp: pulsar decouples stateless brokers from bookkeeper storage, enabling instant broker scaling without data rebalancing. kafka brokers own their partition data on local disk, requiring slow partition reassignment when adding or removing brokers. pulsar offers first-class multi-tenancy through a tenant/namespace/topic hierarchy with per-namespace policies and quotas. pulsar has built-in geo-replication at the namespace level, while kafka relies on the separate mirrormaker 2 tool. pulsar natively supports both streaming (exclusive, failover) and queue (shared, key_shared) subscription types in the same topic. kafka has a far more mature ecosystem with kafka connect, kafka streams, ksqldb, schema registry, and larger community support. choose kafka for raw throughput and ecosystem maturity; choose pulsar for elastic scaling, multi-tenancy, and built-in queue semantics.

kp: kafka hashes the key with murmur2 modulo partition count to assign a record to a partition. same key always maps to the same partition, giving per-key ordering which is critical for banking transactions. a good key has high cardinality and even distribution, such as account id with millions of distinct values. a bad key has low cardinality or heavy skew, such as region or status, funneling most records into one partition. a hot partition bottlenecks one consumer and one broker while others sit idle, and adding consumers does not help. composite keys (account id + bucket number) can spread a dominant key across partitions while preserving partial ordering. changing partition count rehashes keys, so key-to-partition mapping changes and ordering across the boundary is not preserved.

kp: kafka is a durable, replayable, append-only log designed for high-throughput event streaming. rabbitmq is a traditional message broker with amqp exchanges, routing keys, and per-message acknowledgement. kafka retains messages on disk for a configured time regardless of consumption, enabling replay. rabbitmq removes messages from the queue once acknowledged, so there is no built-in replay. kafka uses consumer groups where each group gets the full stream; rabbitmq uses competing consumers on a queue. choose kafka for event sourcing, log aggregation, and stream processing; choose rabbitmq for task queues, rpc, and complex routing. many banks run both: kafka as the event backbone and rabbitmq for targeted task routing and request-reply.

kp: pulsar separates compute (stateless brokers) from storage (apache bookkeeper), allowing independent scaling. pulsar supports four subscription types: exclusive, failover, shared (round-robin, per-message ack), and key-shared. shared subscriptions give rabbitmq-like work-queue semantics from the same topic that also supports streaming. pulsar has first-class multi-tenancy with tenant, namespace, and topic hierarchy and per-namespace policies. built-in geo-replication across clusters is native, unlike kafka which needs separate tooling like mirrormaker 2. kafka has a larger ecosystem, more mature tooling, and more widely available operational expertise. consider pulsar when you need multi-tenancy, unified queue-plus-stream, or simpler geo-replication.

t: How Kafka handles backpressure and its effect on lag and throughput
k: kafka pull model gives backpressure free slow consumer fetches less backlog becomes durable rather overload raise throughput tuning fetch sizes scaling consumers partition count poll request records pace broker never pushes onto unprocessed remain safely bounded retention means growing lost caps many returns bounding batch must process next interval deadline again exceeding triggers rebalance manual offset commit committing processing keeps committed position truthful honestly reflects outstanding work adding raises beyond partitions imagine national bank india documents arriving filing cabinet push
kp: kafka uses a pull model: consumers call poll() to fetch records at their own pace, so a slow consumer simply polls less. unprocessed records remain in the durable log (bounded by retention), so nothing is lost under backpressure. the visible effect of backpressure is consumer lag: the backlog in the log that the consumer has not yet processed. max.poll.records bounds each poll batch; if a batch overruns max.poll.interval.ms the broker triggers a rebalance. manual offset commit (auto.commit=false) keeps lag honest because committed position reflects real completed work. throughput scales by adding consumers up to the partition count; beyond that, add partitions. kafka converts overload into durable lag instead of failure, which buys time to react.

kp: kafka 4.0 fully removed zookeeper and replaced it with kraft (kafka raft metadata mode). kraft stores all cluster metadata in an internal `__cluster_metadata` topic managed by a quorum of controller nodes using the raft consensus protocol. brokers are no longer dependent on an external coordination service; metadata operations are faster and more scalable. kraft supports millions of partitions by eliminating the zookeeper metadata bottleneck. controller quorum sizing follows the same majority-based fault tolerance: three controllers tolerate one failure, five tolerate two. migrating from zookeeper-based kafka to kraft is required before upgrading to kafka 4.0.

kp: git merge creates a merge commit with two parents, preserving the true branching history without rewriting anything. git rebase replays commits onto a new base, creating new commits with new hashes for a clean linear history. merge is non-destructive and safe for shared branches; rebase rewrites history and is safe only on private branches. git stash temporarily shelves uncommitted changes so you can switch branches for urgent work, then pop them back. git cherry-pick copies one specific commit from any branch as a new commit on your current branch. cherry-pick is best for targeted hotfix propagation; overuse across long-lived branches creates duplicated commits. the rule: rebase private branches for clean history, merge shared branches for honest history.

kp: git reset moves the branch pointer backward, dropping commits from the branch -- this rewrites history and is safe only on local, unshared commits. git reset has three modes: --soft keeps changes staged, --mixed keeps them unstaged, --hard discards everything (dangerous). git revert creates a new commit that applies the inverse of a target commit, leaving all history intact -- safe for shared branches. use reset for local undoing, revert for public undoing -- revert preserves the audit trail a bank requires. git reflog records every position head has pointed to, so even after a hard reset, lost commits can be recovered. reflog is local and has an expiry -- unreferenced commits are eventually garbage-collected, so recovery is for recent mistakes. reverting a merge commit requires specifying which parent to keep with the -m flag.

kp: `git merge` creates a merge commit with two parents, preserving the true history of parallel development. `git rebase` replays commits onto another branch tip as new commits, producing a clean linear history but rewriting commit hashes. `git cherry-pick` copies one or more specific commits by hash to the current branch without bringing the rest of the source branch. never rebase commits that have been pushed to a shared branch and pulled by others, because it rewrites shared history and causes divergence. use merge on shared branches for safety, rebase on private branches for cleanliness, and cherry-pick for targeted hotfix transplants or backports. interactive rebase (`git rebase -i`) lets you squash, reorder, edit, or drop commits before replaying, which is ideal for cleaning up a feature branch before review. a common team policy is to rebase locally for clean history and then merge to shared branches with `--no-ff` so shared history is never rewritten.

kp: the working directory is the folder of files you edit on disk; changed files are unstaged until you explicitly add them. the staging area (index) is where you declare exactly which changes go into the next commit, enabling focused, clean commits. the local repository (.git) stores committed snapshots entirely on your machine with no network required. the remote repository (github, gitlab) is the shared copy the whole team uses as the common meeting point. git add moves changes from working directory to staging; git commit saves staging to local repo; git push shares local with remote. git fetch downloads remote changes without touching your working directory; git pull does fetch plus merge in one step. git restore unstages or discards working-directory changes; git reset moves the branch pointer backward.

t: How to do code / PR reviews
k: good review verifies requirement quality correct business logic error handling performance security tests standards catching defects early spreading knowledge check confirming change exactly ticket asked nothing less meaningful names small functions duplication readability future maintainers tracing against realistic cases including boundaries edge exception specific exceptions clean rollback fail-closed behavior sensitive messages watching queries unbounded loading holding connections long parameterized input validation authorization hardcoded secrets test happy path failure assertions think supervisor sign-off large transaction posted national bank india money moves
kp: start by reading the ticket, then the pr description, then the diff -- confirm the change does exactly what was requested, nothing less and nothing more. check business logic by tracing it against realistic cases: money must use bigdecimal, boundaries like zero and negative amounts must be handled. exception handling should be specific, transactions should roll back cleanly, and error messages must not leak sensitive data. security is non-negotiable: parameterized queries, input validation, authorization checks, no hardcoded secrets. tests must cover happy path, failure cases, and boundaries with meaningful assertions; bug fixes need a test that would have caught the bug. performance: watch for n+1 queries, unbounded loops, and holding connections or locks too long. phrase comments as questions, distinguish blockers from nitpicks, praise good work, and review promptly.

kp: the container cgroup memory limit applies to the entire process footprint, not just the java heap. non-heap memory includes metaspace, code cache, thread stacks (around 1 mb each), netty direct buffers, and os page cache. zgc needs more headroom than g1 because it allocates concurrently while reclaiming, and colored pointers add native page-table overhead. set -xmx to about 70-75% of the pod limit for zgc, reserving 25-30% for non-heap and concurrent slack. sizing the heap at 90% leaves no room, so during a gc cycle total rss exceeds the limit and the pod is oomkilled. use maxrampercentage instead of hardcoded -xmx so the heap tracks the container limit automatically.

kp: maven uses declarative xml (pom.xml) with a fixed lifecycle; gradle uses a programmable groovy or kotlin dsl with a directed task graph. maven's lifecycle runs ordered phases -- validate, compile, test, package, verify, install, deploy -- and plugins bind to these phases. gradle's incremental builds skip tasks whose inputs have not changed, the build cache reuses outputs across machines, and the daemon keeps the jvm warm. maven dependency scopes (compile, provided, runtime, test) differ from gradle configurations (implementation, api, compileonly, testimplementation). maven's rigidity makes every project look the same, which is valuable for audits and onboarding in banking. gradle's flexibility and speed suit large multi-module codebases with complex custom build logic. both consume maven central artifacts and resolve transitive dependencies automatically.

kp: maven provides declarative transitive dependency resolution -- you declare one library and maven downloads the entire graph automatically. the standard directory structure (src/main/java, src/test/java, target) means every project looks the same and every ide understands it. the fixed lifecycle (validate, compile, test, package, verify, install, deploy) makes builds repeatable on any machine. a bom (bill of materials) aligns versions of a coordinated set of libraries so you never get transitive version conflicts. scopes (compile, provided, runtime, test) control where each dependency is visible, keeping test-only libraries out of production. the plugin model lets you bind extra work like static analysis, coverage gates, and docker builds to lifecycle phases. maven's discipline -- predictability, auditability, uniformity -- is why regulated industries like banking favor it.

t: Maven lifecycle phases, `mvn install` vs `mvn deploy`, and `distributionManagement`
k: lifecycle runs validate deploy order install publishes your local shared remote repo configured distributionmanagement maven default fixed ordered sequence phases invoking phase executes checks project correct necessary information available compile compiles main source target classes test unit tests fail build stops bundles compiled distributable format verify integration quality copies artifact repository machine uploads nexus artifactory think baking cake national bank india branches recipe check ingredients taste-test inspection distribute putting finished kitchen fridge household sending central bakery warehouse branch country collect
kp: the maven default lifecycle is a fixed ordered chain: validate, compile, test, package, verify, install, deploy -- invoking any phase runs all earlier ones. mvn install builds the artifact and places it into your local .m2 repository so only projects on the same machine can use it. mvn deploy does everything install does and then uploads the artifact to a remote shared repository (nexus or artifactory). distributionmanagement in the pom configures the release and snapshot repository urls that the deploy phase publishes to. snapshot versions end in -snapshot and can be re-published repeatedly; release versions are immutable once published. credentials for the remote repository are stored in settings.xml, never hard-coded in the pom. in a disciplined setup, only the ci server runs mvn deploy so only reviewed, tested artifacts reach the shared repository.

t: What Elasticsearch is, and how it searches internally: inverted index, analyzers, sharding, near-real-time
k: elasticsearch flips problem around instead scanning documents word keeps word-to-documents splits across machines refreshes once distributed document-oriented search analytics engine built apache lucene storing json indices inverted index core structure maps unique term sorted list containing making full-text fast analyzer pipeline character filters tokenizer token transforms text normalized terms during indexing querying sharding splitting pieces primary shards nodes replica fault tolerance read scaling near-real-time newly indexed document becomes searchable refresh interval default instantly imagine back thick banking regulations manual national
kp: elasticsearch is a distributed, document-oriented search and analytics engine built on apache lucene. the inverted index maps each term to the list of documents containing it, which is what makes full-text search fast. analyzers transform text into normalized terms during indexing and querying so searches match regardless of case or word form. sharding splits an index across nodes for horizontal scaling; replica shards provide fault tolerance and read throughput. near-real-time means a newly indexed document becomes searchable after a refresh interval, typically one second. elasticsearch is optimized for read-heavy search and analytics, not for strong transactional consistency.

t: The default mapping type in Elasticsearch (`_doc`) and why multiple types were removed
k: multiple types pretended separate tables secretly shared storage elasticsearch replaced single implicit _doc rule index kind document mapping named sub-grouping documents within loosely analogous table database removed modern fixed name simply lucene root cause removal underlying fields across share definition conflict error occurs define field different entity replacement indices genuinely kinds imagine national bank india once kept savings customers loan ledger book labelled either trouble rows exact column definitions balance money loans remaining principal format clashed eventually said holds exactly
kp: in older elasticsearch, an index could contain multiple mapping types, loosely analogous to tables in a database. from version 7 onward, each index has a single implicit type called _doc. multiple types were removed because all types shared one underlying lucene index, causing field-name conflicts and sparse storage. the replacement is one index per entity kind, each with its own independent field definitions. if documents are variations of the same kind, use a plain field like category to distinguish them instead of types. the lesson is that an abstraction which does not match its implementation is worse than no abstraction.

kp: dynamic mapping creates a multi-field: the top-level field as text (analyzed) plus a .keyword sub-field (exact, ignore_above 256). the text type tokenizes and lowercases for full-text search; the keyword type stores the whole value verbatim for exact match, sort, and aggregation. dynamic mapping hedges because elasticsearch does not know your intent when it first sees a new field. date detection can unexpectedly map date-looking strings as date instead of text. dynamic mapping modes: true (auto-add), runtime, false (ignore), strict (reject unknown fields). for production indices, define explicit mappings rather than relying on dynamic defaults to control size and correctness.

kp: liquibase is an open-source database schema change-management tool that brings version control to the database the way git brings it to code. a changeset is the atomic unit of change, uniquely identified by id, author, and filename, and once applied it is immutable. a changelog is the ordered master file listing changesets; running it against any database applies only what is missing. databasechangelog is a tracking table that records every applied changeset with its checksum, making runs idempotent. databasechangeloglock prevents two instances from migrating simultaneously. liquibase supports expand-and-contract for zero-downtime deployments by ordering changesets across releases.

kp: sdlc is the set of phases every project goes through: requirements, design, implementation, testing, deployment, maintenance. agile is a set of values and principles for running the sdlc iteratively and incrementally in short feedback-driven cycles. sdlc is the what (the phases); agile is a how (one philosophy for executing those phases). waterfall runs the sdlc phases once sequentially; agile runs them in many short iterations. scrum uses fixed sprints with defined roles and ceremonies; kanban uses continuous flow with wip limits. agile only works when paired with ci/cd, automated testing, and devops practices.

kp: serial gc: single-threaded, full stop-the-world, best for tiny heaps and single-core containers. parallel gc: multi-threaded stop-the-world, maximum throughput, best for batch processing (default through java 8). g1: region-based, mostly concurrent, bounded pause target, balanced general-purpose choice (default since java 9). zgc: colored pointers and load barriers, sub-millisecond pauses independent of heap size, best for large-heap latency-critical services. shenandoah: brooks forwarding pointers, concurrent compaction, similar goals to zgc by a different mechanism. collector choice must be measurement-driven: define a latency slo, measure actual pauses, then decide.

t: Why increasing the heap size can make performance WORSE, and why "just raise `-Xmx`" is often the wrong first response
k: bigger heap delays collections makes scan pause longer raising -xmx treats symptom real usually reducing allocation plugging leak choosing right collector flag sets maximum size increasing gives room must live surviving still-reachable objects trace during collection cost scales garbage rate fast application creates high fills even large quickly memory locality close together accesses larger spreads hurts cache performance paging oom-kill exceeds physical swaps disk catastrophically slow container kills process imagine national bank india filing lets clerks pile paperwork anyone tidy
kp: a bigger heap delays collections but makes each one scan more live memory and pause longer. gc cost is proportional to live data (survivors), not to garbage freed. high allocation rate plus large heap gives the worst of both: frequent collections that are also large. a larger heap worsens cpu cache locality and risks os paging or container oom-kill if it exceeds physical ram. the real causes are usually excessive allocation, memory leaks, or the wrong collector: more heap masks symptoms. the correct approach is to diagnose with gc logs, measure allocation rate, and take a heap dump before tuning.

t: How G1GC works: equal-sized regions, dynamic role assignment, Young/Mixed/Concurrent-Marking/Full phases, IHOP, MaxGCPauseMillis: and what makes it "Garbage First"
k: chops heap equal regions greedily collects ones garbage trying stay inside pause-time budget server-style mostly-concurrent region-based collector default since java equal-sized chunks 1-32 dynamically assigned roles eden survivor humongous young collection stop-the-world pause evacuates live objects concurrent marking phase identifies richest mixed plus selected slice trashiest maxgcpausemillis soft target 200ms size generation ihop initiatingheapoccupancypercent threshold triggers imagine bank giant document warehouse split hundreds identical small rooms cleaning crew strict rule minutes clean mostly trash scan throwaway paper empty frees space
kp: g1 divides the heap into many equal-sized regions (1-32 mb) and dynamically assigns each region a role of eden, survivor, old, or humongous. a young collection evacuates live objects from eden and survivor regions in a short stop-the-world pause. concurrent marking runs mostly alongside the application to identify which old regions have the most garbage. a mixed collection evacuates young regions plus the trashiest old regions in one pause: this is literally garbage first. maxgcpausemillis is a soft pause-time target (default 200ms) that g1 uses to size the young generation and mixed collection set. ihop (initiatingheapoccupancypercent) controls when concurrent marking starts; default is 45% and adapts dynamically.

t: The G1 humongous object problem: object larger than 50% of region size: what issues it causes, and how to fix it
k: bigger half region becomes humongous eats whole regions wastes remainder adds pressure single larger heap allocated directly contiguous internal fragmentation wasted space tail last nothing else share external difficulty finding free force full compact g1heapregionsize flag size 1-32 increasing raises threshold worst-case pause triggered cannot find allocation warehouse rooms fixed documents easily occasionally customer submits enormous ledger room rule says giant must locked adjacent even half-fills ledgers keep arriving fragments reserved chunks cleaning crew extra inspections power exactly common causes
kp: any single object larger than 50% of a g1 region is a humongous object allocated directly into contiguous old regions. humongous objects waste the tail of the last region (internal fragmentation) and require contiguous free regions (external fragmentation). a stream of humongous allocations triggers concurrent marking cycles too often and can force a full gc if no contiguous run of free regions is available. fix 1: make the objects smaller by streaming or chunking large payloads. fix 2: increase region size with g1heapregionsize so the object drops below the 50% threshold. fix 3: switch to zgc, whose concurrent relocation handles large objects gracefully.

t: How ZGC achieves sub-millisecond pauses: colored pointers, load barriers, concurrent relocation, self-healing references: and what Generational ZGC is
k: keeps pauses under millisecond marking moving objects concurrently colored pointers plus load barriers references self-heal location read scalable low-latency mostly-concurrent garbage collector whose stop-the-world stay regardless heap size metadata stored spare bits 64-bit reference marked remapped generation small jit-inserted checks color fixes relocated self-healing property corrected once cycle touch concurrent relocation compacts application runs lazily repoint generational young split efficiency opt-in java default exclusive imagine renovating bank customers keep transacting crew moves desk background file coloured sticker says moved teller
kp: zgc keeps pauses under a millisecond regardless of heap size by doing marking and relocation concurrently with the application. colored pointers store gc metadata (marked, remapped) in spare bits of the 64-bit reference. load barriers check the color on every reference load; if the object has moved, the barrier transparently fixes the reference. self-healing means each reference is corrected at most once per cycle, spreading the cost smoothly instead of one long pause. generational zgc splits the heap into young and old generations so most work targets short-lived objects. generational zgc was opt-in in java 21, default in java 23, and the only mode in java 24 via jep 490.

t: Why ZGC can still show a huge periodic latency spike: the allocation stall: how ZUncommit worsens bursty workloads, and how to fix it
k: pauses stay tiny allocation outruns reclamation stalls waiting memory zuncommit makes bursts worse forcing re-commit fixed heap pre-touch generational mode stall application rate outpaces concurrent allocating thread parked until freed pause feature returns unused pages during quiet periods reduce resident footprint page faults zeroing cost re-acquiring committed burst arrives adds latency worst moment alwayspretouch flag zeroes startup paying once instead live collects young generation frequently cheaply keeping free space ahead renovation crew normally works background without stopping customers sudden rush
kp: an allocation stall happens when the application allocates faster than zgc can concurrently reclaim, so threads are parked waiting for free memory. zgc's sub-millisecond guarantee is about gc pauses, not about application waits from running out of memory. zuncommit returns unused heap to the os during quiet periods, but re-committing pages during a burst causes page faults and zeroing. fix 1: set -xms equal to -xmx to disable uncommit and keep the heap fixed. fix 2: add alwayspretouch to fault in all pages at startup so bursts never pay page-fault costs. fix 3: use generational zgc (default from java 23) so the young generation is collected frequently and free space stays ahead of allocation.

kp: shenandoah is red hat's low-pause, mostly-concurrent collector that performs concurrent compaction while the application runs. the brooks forwarding pointer is an extra reference-sized word per object that always points to the object's current location. read and write barriers follow the forwarding pointer so accesses always reach the current copy during relocation. stop-the-world pauses are limited to short init-mark and final-mark handshakes, independent of heap size. generational shenandoah (jep 521, java 25) adds young/old generations so most work targets short-lived objects. enable with -xx:+useshenandoahgc; generational mode with -xx:shenandoahgcmode=generational on java 25.

kp: epsilon is a no-op garbage collector that allocates memory but never reclaims it (java 11, jep 318). when the heap is exhausted, the jvm throws outofmemoryerror or terminates: there is no collection. epsilon is ideal for benchmarking because it removes all gc noise from performance measurements. it measures true allocation rate: run a fixed workload and see how fast the heap fills. short-lived programs that finish before the heap fills get maximum throughput with zero pauses. epsilon is explicitly not for production services; it is a measurement and specialization tool.

kp: devsecops integrates security into every stage of the delivery lifecycle as a shared, automated responsibility. shift left moves security activities earlier so vulnerabilities are found when they are cheapest to fix. a manual end-gate cannot keep up with high release cadence and either blocks velocity or gets waived. pipeline security stages include secret scanning, sast, sca, container scanning, and policy checks on every commit. the cost of fixing a defect rises steeply at each stage from design to coding to testing to production. shift left does not mean shift-left-only: runtime protection and production monitoring are still needed.

t: The difference between SAST, DAST, IAST, and SCA: and where each runs in the SDLC
k: sast reads your checks dependencies iast watches inside during tests dast attacks running outside catching different flaw sdlc stage application security testing analyzes source bytecode without finding code-level flaws injection hardcoded secrets early build dynamic attacker runtime configuration deployed environment interactive instruments agent functional combining insight context software composition analysis inventories third-party open-source flags known vulnerabilities license risks complementary shift left runs validates relying leaves blind spot imagine securing national bank india branch architect reviewing blueprints mistakes anything built checking
kp: sast analyzes source code without running it, catching code-level flaws like sql injection and hardcoded secrets early in the build. dast tests the running application from the outside like an attacker, finding runtime and configuration flaws with few false positives. iast instruments the running application with an agent during tests, combining code-level precision with runtime confidence. sca inventories third-party dependencies and flags known vulnerabilities and license risks; most real-world vulnerabilities enter through dependencies. sast and sca run in the build for fast per-commit feedback; iast runs during integration testing; dast runs against a deployed environment. these are complementary, not competing: each catches a class of flaw the others miss.

kp: an sbom is a machine-readable inventory of every direct and transitive component in your software, with names, versions, suppliers, and hashes. spdx is the iso-standardized format from the linux foundation; cyclonedx is the owasp format designed for security use cases. the operational value appears when a vulnerability drops: you query your sboms to instantly find which services are affected. sboms are generated automatically in the build pipeline and stored in a central index keyed by service and version. pairing sboms with a continuous vulnerability feed alerts you when a library you shipped months ago becomes dangerous. an sbom that a tool can parse and query is useful; a pdf a human must read is not.

kp: oidc federation replaces long-lived cloud keys with short-lived tokens exchanged for temporary credentials that expire in minutes. ephemeral runners are destroyed after each job, preventing secrets or malware from persisting between builds. pinning third-party actions to exact commit shas prevents a moved tag from injecting malicious code into your pipeline. least-privilege deploy roles limit the blast radius if a pipeline is compromised. an internal artifact registry with dependency pinning and checksum verification defends against supply-chain and dependency-confusion attacks. artifact signing with provenance attestations ensures only trusted, verified artifacts are deployed.

kp: blocking on every high/critical finding floods developers with noise and causes them to bypass the gate entirely. the strongest blocking criterion combines severity (cvss), reachability (does your code call the vulnerable function?), and exploitability (cisa kev, epss). remediation slas by severity: critical within 72 hours, high within 30 days, medium within 90 days, low within 180 days. the gate stops new critical issues from entering; the sla process drives down the existing backlog over time. exceptions are time-boxed, signed, and expiring: who requested, who approved, justification, compensating control, and expiry date. an exception that expires automatically forces re-review and produces an auditable trail for regulators.

t: Explain the Shared Responsibility Model, and why most cloud breaches are on the customer side (misconfiguration, over-permissioned identities)
k: provider secures cloud secure nearly breach someone leaving unlocked responsibility security physical centers hardware hypervisor managed-service control plane customer identity access configuration network rules encryption settings patching application service model shift iaas guest paas takes runtime saas your scope narrows never zero always pattern failures misconfiguration over-permissioned identities bank building rents safe-deposit vault door walls guards alarm given decide whether lock hand copies national india leaves wide open money stolen builder fault shared contract divides duties responsible dividing line exact
kp: the provider secures the cloud (data centers, hardware, hypervisor); the customer secures what they put in the cloud (data, identity, config). the dividing line moves by service model: iaas puts os and above on you; paas/managed services shrink your scope; saas narrows it to access and data. your responsibility never drops to zero: in every model you always own your data and your identity-and-access configuration. most breaches are customer-side because the provider's half is hardened at scale while the customer's half is bespoke and error-prone. the two dominant failures are misconfiguration (public buckets, default passwords) and over-permissioned identities (wildcard policies). defenses: infrastructure-as-code, posture scanning, least privilege, short-lived credentials, encryption by default, and guardrail policies.

kp: six pillars: operational excellence, security, reliability, performance efficiency, cost optimization, and sustainability. each pillar is an independent lens on the same design, asking a different question about the workload. the pillars deliberately pull against each other: reliability raises cost, performance tempts over-provisioning, security can add latency. a review produces a prioritized list of risks (high/medium/low) with owners and follow-up dates, not a score. the output that matters is the ranked list of risks and the commitment to fix the top ones before launch. reviews are repeatable and periodic because architecture drifts over time.

kp: rto is the maximum acceptable downtime; rpo is the maximum acceptable data loss. both are business decisions. backup and restore: cheapest, hours of rto, rpo equals backup frequency. pilot light: database replicating, compute off; moderate cost, shorter rto, low rpo. warm standby: scaled-down but fully functional copy; higher cost, minutes of rto. multi-site active/active: full production in multiple regions; highest cost, near-zero rto and rpo. an untested dr plan is a hypothesis: documentation decays silently and only surfaces during a real outage.

kp: retire (decommission) and retain (leave for now) reduce migration scope before spending anything on moving. rehost (lift-and-shift) moves to the cloud with no code changes: fast, low-risk, but captures only basic benefits. replatform (lift-tinker-and-shift) makes targeted optimizations like moving to a managed database, without changing the core architecture. refactor (re-architect) is the deepest strategy: breaking monoliths into microservices or going serverless for maximum cloud benefit. repurchase replaces self-managed software with a saas subscription. choose per application by scoring business value, technical complexity, cloud suitability, cost, and risk: never one r for the whole estate.

kp: systems manager (ssm) is a broad operations-management service: run command, session manager, parameter store, inventory, state manager, and automation. patch manager is one feature inside ssm, specialized for applying os and application patches using baselines and maintenance windows. the ssm agent polls outbound over https, so no inbound ports need to be opened: session manager gives shell access without ssh keys. parameter store holds configuration and kms-encrypted secrets; the application reads them at startup instead of hardcoding credentials. patch baselines define which patches are approved; patch groups tag instances to a baseline; maintenance windows schedule when patching runs. patch manager depends on ssm being set up first: the agent, the instance role, and connectivity to ssm endpoints.

t: (Scenario) Cross-account AWS Lambda in Account B using Amazon EFS owned by Account A: why it needs both network connectivity and authorization, and why SCPs or cross-region role assumption do NOT solve it
k: cross-account lambda needs network path peering authorization resource policy execution-role permissions scps restrict role assumption wrong tool entirely connectivity mount targets live specific must reach transit gateway port open file granting account execution clientmount clientwrite client networking required axes fail independently without gives access-denied timeout trap service control policies never grant create paths mounting authorized plus assuming imagine national bank india central records vault partner branch courier read ledger things physical road connecting access list allowed enter means cannot door
kp: efs is mounted over nfs (tcp port 2049) to a mount target in a specific vpc: the lambda must have a network path to that vpc. network connectivity requires vpc peering or transit gateway with routes and security groups allowing nfs on port 2049. authorization requires an efs resource policy allowing account b's execution role, plus efs client and vpc permissions on the role. both axes fail independently: correct network without authorization gives access-denied; correct authorization without network gives timeout. scps can only restrict, never grant permissions or build network routes, so they solve neither problem. cross-region role assumption is the wrong mechanism: efs access is authorized by resource policy plus network path, not identity swap.

t: When to use OkHttp MockWebServer versus WebTestClient: testing outbound HTTP calls versus testing your own reactive controllers

kp: mockwebserver tests outbound calls your service makes to downstream services; webtestclient tests inbound requests your own controllers receive. mockwebserver is a real http server on a local port: you enqueue scripted responses and assert the exact request your code sent. mockwebserver shines at simulating downstream failure: 500s for retry logic, 404s for exception mapping, delays for timeout verification. webtestclient with @webfluxtest loads only the web layer, mocks service collaborators, and verifies routing, validation, and response serialization. the two are complementary, not competing: use both in the same test suite for different seams. choosing the wrong tool is a classic mistake: mockwebserver tells you nothing about your routing; webtestclient tells you nothing about your outbound client.

kp: a ci/cd pipeline is an automated sequence of stages that carries a code change from commit to a running environment. typical stages are source, build, test, package, scan, deploy, and verify, each gating the next. continuous integration merges, builds, and tests every change automatically and frequently. continuous delivery automates everything up to a production-ready artifact but keeps a manual approval before production. continuous deployment removes the manual gate and releases every green build to production automatically. the artifact must be immutable, tagged with the commit sha, and promoted unchanged across environments.

kp: secrets must never live in source code, build logs, or image layers. store secrets in a dedicated manager like hashicorp vault, aws secrets manager, or the ci system's encrypted store. inject secrets at runtime as masked environment variables or mounted files, scoped only to the step that needs them. never bake secrets into docker images with env or copy because image layers are readable and persistent. prefer short-lived, dynamically issued credentials (oidc federation) over long-lived static keys. wire a pre-commit secret scanner like gitleaks into ci so the build fails if a secret is ever committed.

kp: sonarqube analyses code for bugs, smells, and security hotspots, and enforces a quality gate that fails the build if thresholds are not met. trivy and grype scan container images and dependencies against cve databases and fail the build on severe findings. nexus and artifactory store build outputs as immutable versions and proxy external repositories through a controlled, cached gateway. sast analyses source code without running it, catching insecure patterns early on every commit. dast scans a running application from the outside with real http requests, finding runtime flaws like injection and auth bypasses. these tools are complementary layers: sast finds code issues, scanners find dependency issues, dast finds runtime issues.

kp: the amazon vpc cni gives each pod a real, routable vpc ip address, so each pod consumes one subnet ip. the cni pre-allocates warm ips per node for fast pod startup, so reserved ips far exceed active pod count. ip exhaustion blocks new pods from starting (containercreating with cni errors) even when cpu and memory are available. fix: add subnets or a secondary vpc cidr, enable prefix delegation, tune warm pool settings, consider ipv6. monitor subnet free-ip counts proactively and alert before utilization gets high. this is a design consequence of the native-ip model and must be planned at vpc-design time.

kp: always separate immediate mitigation (restore service fast) from the longer-term fix (prevent recurrence), and always mitigate first. for ec2 failing alb health checks: let auto scaling replace unhealthy instances, then fix the readiness endpoint and tune grace periods. for rds storage exhaustion: grow storage online or enable autoscaling immediately, then add cloudwatch alarms and data retention policies. for a failed production deployment: roll back to the last known-good version immediately, then close the pipeline gap with staging gates and canary delivery. every minute of outage costs customers and money, so restore service first and do root-cause analysis only after the system is stable. a senior engineer always keeps the previous version warm and deployments reversible so rollback is instantaneous.

kp: aws list apis cap results per response (often 50-1000 items) and return a `nexttoken` when more exist; you must loop until no token remains. ignoring the token is a silent, large-account-only bug: the script returns partial results with no error, making it the most dangerous kind of automation failure. a boto3 paginator (`get_paginator(...).paginate()`) encapsulates the token loop correctly, yielding each page until the end, so you always get complete results. manual token loops are error-prone: common bugs include a `while token` loop that never runs because the token starts empty, and forgetting to accumulate results across pages. paginators integrate with boto3's retry configuration, so transient errors mid-traversal are retried automatically, making the full traversal robust as well as complete. in banking, incomplete results mean cost reports understate spend, compliance scans miss untagged instances, and cleanup jobs skip resources.

kp: a feature flag is a runtime switch that turns functionality on or off without a redeploy, decoupling deployment from release. flags enable testing in production by exposing a feature only to internal users or a small percentage while watching real behavior. instant rollback is the standout benefit: flipping a flag off disables a feature in seconds with no redeploy or rollback pipeline. flag types include release flags (gradual rollout), kill switches (disable under load), experiment flags (a/b tests), and permission flags (user segments). flags must be evaluated consistently per user (stable bucketing) and have a safe default so a flag-service outage does not break requests. release flags must be removed promptly after full rollout, because unmanaged flags accumulate into technical debt.

t: What an SLO is and what an SLI is
k: actual measured quality service user perspective target must meet measurement versus goal level indicator precisely defined quantity reflecting percentage successful requests served faster latency threshold objective period days defining reliable enough means relationship error budget minus amount unreliability permitted external contract penalties internal usually stricter national bank india think reliability punctuality branch hundred customers month many were successfully quickly promise sets itself least number stays above meeting drops below failing standard ratio good events total valid keeps makes directly comparable
kp: an sli (service level indicator) is a precisely defined, measured quantity reflecting service quality from the user's perspective, such as the percentage of successful requests. an slo (service level objective) is a target value for an sli over a period, such as 99.9% of requests successful over 30 days. each additional nine is dramatically more expensive: 99.9% allows ~8.7 hours downtime per year, 99.99% allows ~52 minutes, 99.999% allows ~5 minutes. slis should be measured at the point closest to the user (load balancer or gateway) and defined as good events over total valid events. the sli and slo together produce an error budget: the amount of unreliability the slo permits (100% minus the slo target). an slo is an internal target; an sla is an external contract with customers, usually set looser than the slo for safety margin.

kp: an error budget is 100% minus the slo target: if the slo is 99.9%, the error budget is 0.1% of requests (or time) that may fail over the window. the budget quantifies acceptable failure, turning reliability into a consumable resource that teams spend on deployment risk and feature velocity. when budget remains, the team ships features and takes reasonable risk; when the budget is exhausted, risky feature work is frozen and the focus shifts to reliability. alert on burn rate (how fast the budget is being consumed), not on every transient blip: a fast burn pages immediately, a slow burn raises a ticket. the error budget resolves the tension between product (ship fast) and operations (stay stable) with data instead of opinion. the budget is a steering tool, not a stick: consistently exhausting it signals a need to invest in reliability or relax an over-strict slo.

kp: incident management is a five-step lifecycle: detect, triage, respond, fix (mitigate first), and blameless postmortem. detection must be automated and tied to user-facing signals (error rate, latency), not internal metrics that do not reflect customer impact. triage assesses severity and scope: what is broken, for how many users, since when, and is it getting worse. response assigns clear roles: incident commander (coordinates), responders (investigate), communicator (updates stakeholders). the fix phase follows the cardinal rule: mitigate first to restore service, then do root-cause analysis after the system is stable. the blameless postmortem documents what happened, why, and concrete action items to prevent recurrence, focusing on systems rather than blaming individuals.

kp: first confirm and size the actual user impact using dashboards and user-facing slis, not a single component's status. look for what changed most recently (deploy, config, feature flag, infra change) because a recent change is both the most likely cause and the fastest thing to undo. mitigate first to restore service: rollback, flag flip, scale out, failover, or shed load; do not try to understand the cause during the outage. rollback is usually the fastest safe mitigation because it returns the system to a known-good state without requiring diagnosis. communicate status continuously: silence during an outage destroys trust faster than the outage itself. deep root-cause analysis and blameless postmortem happen only after service is restored, because investigating a stable system is calm, safe, and thorough.

t: What a blameless postmortem is and why it is blameless
k: blameless postmortem honest after-incident document focused fixing systems rather blaming people psychological safety produces truthful account needed prevent recurrence written retrospective produced incident documenting happened timeline impact resolved action items deliberately framed analyze systemic process causes assign individual fault fear punishment minimize distort hiding information real cause human error reframing mistake treated symptom weakness missing guardrail confusing tooling root accountability team accountable completing individuals blamed mistakes competent person made serious mix-up national bank india writes report went wrong many customers
kp: a blameless postmortem is a written retrospective that documents what happened, the timeline, root cause, impact, and concrete action items to prevent recurrence. it is blameless because the aim is organizational learning: when people fear punishment, they hide information, which prevents fixing the real cause. human error is treated as a symptom of a deeper systemic weakness, not the root cause: the question is why the system allowed a single mistake to cause damage. action items must be concrete, owned, and time-bound, or the postmortem changes nothing. blameless does not mean no accountability: the team is accountable for completing action items and improving the system. psychological safety produces the honest, detailed account needed to uncover real causes like missing guardrails, inadequate tests, and unclear runbooks.

kp: rollingupdate replaces pods incrementally, keeping old pods serving traffic until new pods pass readiness probes, achieving zero downtime. recreate terminates every old pod before starting any new pod, guaranteeing a downtime window but ensuring only one version runs at a time. maxsurge controls how many extra pods above the desired count are allowed during a roll; maxunavailable controls how many may be missing. rollingupdate requires backward-compatible code and schema because two versions briefly coexist. recreate suits singletons and incompatible upgrades where two versions must never overlap. readiness probes, graceful shutdown, and expand-and-contract schema migrations are prerequisites for genuine zero downtime with rollingupdate.

kp: recreate kills old pods then starts new ones: downtime guaranteed, no version overlap, lowest cost. rolling replaces pods incrementally: zero downtime, slow rollback, two versions coexist briefly. blue-green runs two full environments and flips a load-balancer switch: instant cutover and fastest rollback, at double infrastructure cost. canary shifts a small percentage of traffic to the new version while watching metrics: lowest risk, fast abort. shadow mirrors production traffic to the new version but discards its responses: zero user risk, validates performance under real load. zero downtime is an objective, not a strategy, because rolling, blue-green, canary, and shadow can all achieve it by different mechanisms. expand-and-contract keeps schema changes safe: add new structure first, migrate data, remove old structure only after all old code is gone.

kp: before container awareness, the jvm sized itself from host memory, causing pods to be oom-killed when the cgroup limit was exceeded. -xx:+usecontainersupport (on by default since java 10, backported to 8u191) makes the jvm read cgroup memory and cpu limits. -xx:maxrampercentage sets the heap as a fraction of the container limit, typically 75% to leave room for non-heap memory. setting kubernetes memory request equal to limit gives the pod guaranteed qos class and prevents overcommit kills. -xx:+exitonoutofmemoryerror terminates the jvm cleanly on oom so kubernetes restarts the pod to a known-good state. always verify at startup that the effective heap reflects the cgroup limit, not the host.

kp: hpa scales the number of pod replicas based on cpu, memory, or custom metrics. vpa scales each pod up by adjusting its cpu and memory requests and limits based on observed usage. cluster autoscaler scales the number of nodes when pods cannot be scheduled for lack of capacity. keda scales replicas based on external event sources like kafka lag or queue depth, and can scale to zero. hpa and vpa must not both manage the same cpu or memory metric on the same workload, or they oscillate. hpa and cluster autoscaler are a natural pair: hpa creates more pods, cluster autoscaler adds more nodes.

kp: a configmap stores non-sensitive configuration as key-value pairs such as feature flags, log levels, and timeouts. a secret stores sensitive data like database passwords and api keys, base64-encoded and ideally encrypted at rest. environment variable injection is read once at container start, so changes never take effect without a pod restart. volume-mounted configmaps are refreshed on disk by the kubelet, but subpath mounts never update. most applications cache config at startup, so even refreshed files on disk do not change behaviour without a reload. the safest pattern is immutable, versioned configmaps referenced from the pod template so rollback reverts config too.

kp: `like '%term%'` with a leading wildcard forces a full sequential scan because a b-tree index is ordered by prefix and cannot seek to an arbitrary position. a trailing wildcard like `like 'term%'` can use a b-tree index because the match starts at a known prefix. full-text search uses a `tsvector` of normalized, stemmed tokens and a gin inverted index that maps each token to its rows. stemming means a search for "payment" also matches "payments" and "paying," which like cannot do. relevance ranking with `ts_rank` orders results by match quality, not just presence. elasticsearch is for distributed full-text search at scale with fuzzy matching, faceting, and custom analyzers. keep the tsvector as a stored generated column with a gin index so lookups are fast and stay in sync automatically.

kp: a candidate key is any minimal set of columns that uniquely identifies a row, and a table can have several. a natural key is a candidate key made of real-world attributes like pan or email that exist independently of the database. a surrogate key is an artificial, meaningless identifier like an auto-increment integer or uuid generated solely to be the primary key. when one candidate key is chosen as primary, every other candidate key becomes an alternate key enforced with a unique constraint. production schemas prefer surrogate keys because they are stable, meaningless, narrow, and never change. natural keys leak sensitive data into foreign keys, urls, and logs, creating privacy and compliance problems. keep natural keys as unique constraints so the database still prevents duplicate emails or pans.
