kp: oltp handles many small, fast, concurrent transactions with normalized schemas and row-oriented storage. olap handles complex analytical queries over large historical data with star schemas and column-oriented storage. oltp uses indexes for fast point lookups; olap uses columnar scans for aggregations. running heavy analytics on the production db starves latency-sensitive transactions of cpu, memory, and i/o. a row-store forced to aggregate one column across millions of rows reads every column of every row, which is slow. separate them via etl, elt, or change-data-capture into a warehouse or lake. read replicas or streaming keep the analytics copy seconds behind for near-real-time needs.

t: Schema-on-write vs schema-on-read
k: schema-on-write enforces structure storing clean fast queries schema-on-read stores applies read maximum flexibility types defined enforced stored must conform write relational database as-is schema applied files lake integrity guarantee valid provides automatically evolution changing adding columns without breaking existing self-describing format formats parquet embed file providing hybrid approach registry central service versioned schemas compatibility rules even lakes national bank india account-opening form detail filed field filled correctly name amount number clerk rejects anything wrong miscellaneous documents staff toss letters screenshots
kp: schema-on-write enforces structure and types before data is stored, as in a relational database. schema-on-read stores raw data as-is and applies the schema only when the data is queried. schema-on-write guarantees data integrity and fast queries but is rigid and slow to change. schema-on-read is flexible and fast for ingestion but bad data is only discovered at read time. parquet is a hybrid: it carries its own schema in the footer, giving read-time structure with strong typing. mature lakes still register schemas in a catalog with compatibility rules even with schema-on-read. banks use both deliberately: schema-on-read for raw ingestion speed, schema-on-write for regulated reporting trust.

t: Schema evolution in a data pipeline and why columnar formats matter
k: evolve schemas safely versioned formats registry compatibility rules columnar parquet analytics prunes columns pushes down filters compresses hard schema evolution managing changes structure adding removing changing fields without breaking existing producers consumers central service stores version enforces registration backward read written consumer forward column pruning reading query needs file skipping rest entirely predicate pushdown per-block statistics skip blocks cannot match filter national bank india keeps transaction slip years year channel field mobile versus branch another drop unused making sure reader
kp: schema evolution manages changes to data structure over time without breaking producers or consumers. avro embeds the writer's schema in the file header; parquet embeds its schema in the file footer. a schema registry stores versioned schemas and enforces backward, forward, or full compatibility rules. safe changes: add fields with defaults, deprecate old fields. unsafe: rename in place, change types. column pruning lets parquet read only the columns a query needs, cutting i/o by orders of magnitude. predicate pushdown uses per-row-group min/max statistics to skip irrelevant data without decompression. same-type column values compress far better than mixed-type rows, reducing both storage cost and scan time.

kp: oltp is a normalized row-store for fast point writes; olap is a denormalized column-store star schema for big scans. row-store keeps all columns of a row together, ideal for reading or writing one whole row at a time. column-store keeps all values of one column together, ideal for aggregating a few columns across millions of rows. normalized schemas prevent update anomalies; star schemas trade redundancy for simple analytical joins. separation is essential because heavy scans contend for cpu, memory, and i/o that transactions need. etl, elt, or change-data-capture moves data from oltp to olap, isolating the workloads. htap systems attempt both on one engine, but banks prefer clear separation for safety.

kp: batch processing collects data into a bounded dataset and processes the whole chunk in one scheduled run. stream processing handles an unbounded sequence of events continuously as each arrives. batch optimizes for throughput and cost; streaming optimizes for low latency. streaming must deal with event-time vs processing-time, late data, and watermarks that batch sidesteps. spark structured streaming uses micro-batch (tiny stacks); flink uses true record-at-a-time for lowest latency. lambda architecture combines batch and stream layers; kappa uses stream-only for simplicity. banks use both: streaming for real-time fraud alerts, batch for complete daily reports.

kp: spark batch processes a bounded dataset in scheduled runs, optimizing for throughput with catalyst and tungsten. spark structured streaming uses micro-batch: tiny bounded batches triggered at short intervals, reusing spark's optimizer. flink uses true record-at-a-time: each event flows through operators individually for lowest latency. micro-batch has a latency floor equal to the trigger interval (hundreds of milliseconds to seconds). record-at-a-time can achieve low-millisecond latency with precise event-time handling and rich keyed state. use batch for nightly reports; micro-batch for near-real-time dashboards; flink for fraud blocking under tight latency. the line has blurred: spark added continuous mode, flink supports batch over bounded streams.

kp: stateful streaming remembers information across events, unlike stateless processing that treats each event independently. keyed state is state scoped per key (e.g., per trading symbol), with all events for one key routed to the same place. windowed aggregations bound the infinite stream into finite pieces: tumbling (fixed, non-overlapping) or sliding (overlapping). the state backend stores keyed state: in-memory for speed or rocksdb for large state that exceeds ram. checkpointing periodically snapshots all state plus source offsets for exactly-once fault tolerance. top 5 symbols by volume: key by symbol, sum volume in 1-min tumbling window, rank at window close. manage state size with time-to-live so stale keys are evicted and do not consume resources.

k: parquet stores column analytics reads columns needs skips irrelevant compresses better formats apache open-source columnar storage file format optimized analytical workloads layout storing values together instead pruning reading query skipping rest entirely predicate pushdown per-row-group statistics skip blocks cannot match filter group horizontal partition contains chunks self-describing footer holds full schema per-column imagine national bank india keeps giant ledger hundred transaction account amount timestamp branch device ninety-six row-based book page complete fields total must flip re-filing amounts slim folder branches
kp: parquet is a columnar file format that stores values column by column instead of row by row. column pruning reads only the columns a query needs, cutting i/o by orders of magnitude on wide tables. predicate pushdown uses per-row-group min/max statistics to skip irrelevant blocks without decompression. same-type column values compress far better than mixed-type rows via dictionary and run-length encoding. parquet is self-describing: the file footer holds the full schema and statistics. parquet is write-once, read-many: it pairs with delta lake or iceberg for acid and updates. it is the de facto format for data lakes and big-data engines like spark, trino, and hive.

t: Transformations vs actions and lazy evaluation
k: transformations build lazy plan dataset actions execute result evaluation lets spark optimize whole chain running transformation operation takes dataframe returns building logical without executing filter join select distinct action eager triggers execution accumulated writes output collect count show write principle record intent until forces optimized catalyst optimizer query planner benefits push filters prune columns reorder joins narrow movement needed partition depends input wide requires shuffle across network groupbykey imagine manager national bank india writing to-do list processing statements rajesh transactions
kp: transformations are lazy: they build a logical plan and return a new dataset without executing anything. actions are eager: they trigger execution of the accumulated plan and return a result or write output. lazy evaluation lets spark's catalyst optimizer push filters, prune columns, fuse maps, and reorder joins. narrow transformations (map, filter) need no shuffle; wide transformations (groupbykey, join) require a shuffle. each action re-triggers the whole lineage, so calling two actions on an uncached chain recomputes everything twice. a quick rule: if the return type is a dataframe/rdd, it is a transformation; if it returns a value or writes, it is an action. cache before multiple actions to avoid redundant recomputation of the same intermediate result.

kp: parquet stores min/max statistics per column chunk at the row-group and page level for range-based skipping. if a filter value falls outside a row group's min/max range, the entire group is skipped without decompression. dictionary filtering checks the dictionary page for equality predicates and skips blocks missing the value. bloom filters provide probabilistic "definitely not present" checks for high-cardinality columns like transaction id. sorted data produces tight, non-overlapping min/max ranges per block, making statistics actually skip blocks. unsorted data gives wide overlapping ranges that span the full domain, rendering statistics useless. min/max and dictionary are on by default; bloom filters must be enabled per column at write time.

kp: avro is row-based with schema in the file header, ideal for write-heavy ingestion and schema evolution. parquet is columnar with column pruning and predicate pushdown, the default for read-heavy analytics. orc is columnar with built-in indexes and hive acid support for row-level updates on analytical tables. avro pairs with a schema registry for kafka pipelines; parquet pairs with spark and cloud lakehouses. you do not analyze directly on avro because columnar scans touch a fraction of the bytes. you do not stream individual events into parquet because columnar formats want large batched writes. common pattern: land raw as avro for cheap evolvable writes, curate as parquet for fast analytical reads.

t: What is Delta Lake and how it differs from plain Parquet

kp: delta lake is parquet plus a transaction log (_delta_log) that turns a folder of files into an acid table. each commit is an atomic set of actions (add/remove files) recorded as a numbered json file in the log. readers reconstruct the table at version n by replaying commits 0 through n. optimistic concurrency control handles concurrent writers: only one can create the next log entry. schema enforcement rejects writes with wrong columns or types; schema evolution is opt-in with mergeschema. time travel lets you query any prior version with versionasof or timestampasof. vacuum removes old files after a retention period, freeing storage used by time travel.

kp: spark dataframes are distributed, immutable, and lazily evaluated: transformations build a plan, actions trigger execution. pandas dataframes are single-machine, in-memory, and eager: every operation executes immediately. lazy evaluation lets catalyst see the entire chain and optimize it before data moves (predicate pushdown, column pruning, join reordering). each action re-runs the plan from the start unless you cache or persist the intermediate dataframe. wide transformations (join, groupby) require a shuffle; narrow transformations (filter, select) do not. null handling in spark uses dropna, fillna, and when/otherwise for conditional column logic. use pandas for small interactive work and spark when data outgrows one machine.

kp: every rdd is defined by five internal properties: partitions, compute function, dependencies, optional partitioner, and preferred locations. the list of partitions sets the unit of parallelism, with one task created per partition per stage. the compute function tells spark how to produce each partition on demand, either from storage or by transforming a parent. dependencies form the lineage and come in two kinds: narrow (no shuffle, pipeline-able) and wide (shuffle, stage boundary). an optional partitioner like hashpartitioner or rangepartitioner controls how keys map to partitions in key-value rdds. preferred locations are data-locality hints that spark uses to schedule tasks close to their data: process_local, node_local, rack_local, any. these five properties explain almost every spark performance question: partition count drives parallelism, dependencies drive shuffles, and the partitioner can eliminate shuffles.

kp: predicate pushdown pushes filter conditions to the data source so rows are eliminated before entering spark executor memory. for parquet and orc, the source uses per-row-group min/max statistics to skip entire row groups whose range cannot match the filter. for jdbc sources, the predicate becomes a sql where clause executed by the database using its own indexes. for row-based csv and json, there are no column statistics, so the reader must parse every row before applying the filter. pushdown only works for predicates the source understands: simple comparisons, equality, in, and ranges on columns. non-deterministic functions and user-defined functions usually cannot be pushed down and run in spark after the full read. verify pushdown happened by calling explain() and reading the pushedfilters line on the scan node.

t: Data skew in Spark: hot keys and how to detect it
k: skew partition holding rest creating straggler task spot spark taking hundred times longer lopsided shuffle sizes uneven distribution across partitions hold records join group appears disproportionately often funneling rows single processing oversized runs much peers delaying whole stage detection stages maximum duration median read larger others root cause wide operation groupby repartition hashes skewed creates imbalance national bank india imagine distributing transactions clerks account number accounts corporate mega-account millions clerk handling buried hours finishes minutes sits idle batch done until
kp: data skew is uneven data distribution across partitions after a shuffle, caused by a hot key that appears disproportionately often. one oversized partition creates a straggler task that delays the entire stage because the stage cannot finish until its slowest task completes. detect skew in the spark ui stages tab by comparing maximum task duration to the median – a ratio of ten to a hundred times indicates skew. the straggler task also shows a much larger shuffle read than its peers and may spill to disk or fail with out-of-memory. profile the hot key by grouping on the join or group column and counting rows per key to surface dominant values. common banking hot keys include sweep accounts, suspense accounts, default placeholder ids, and null keys collecting all unmatched rows. distinguish skew from too few partitions: skew makes one task large while others are tiny, whereas too few partitions makes every task roughly equally large.

t: Salting: spreading a hot key across partitions, and the trade-off
k: salting appends random suffix spread across partitions replicates side times still match trading duplicated balanced manual skew-mitigation technique number salt skewed join large splitting composite keys explosion small replicated once finds trade-off count shuffle memory footprint multiply balance carefully targeted apply known limit duplication rather entire dataset two-stage aggregation groupby operations aggregate salted re-aggregate values total national bank india pooling account millions transactions pile onto clerk sub-labels plus zero nine sprinkling clerks matching work reference record must copied need heavy
kp: salting appends a random integer (0 to n-1) to the hot join key on the large side, turning one key into n composite keys spread across n partitions. the small side must be exploded into n copies, one per salt value, so each composite key still finds its match. after the join, the salt column is dropped to recover the original logical result. the trade-off is replication: exploding the small side by n multiplies its row count, shuffle size, and memory footprint by n. targeted salting applies the salt only to known hot keys and leaves cold keys unsalted, controlling the duplication cost. for a skewed groupby, salting requires a two-stage aggregation: aggregate per salted key first, then re-aggregate across salts. try adaptive query execution skew join optimization first; reach for manual salting only when aqe is insufficient.

kp: executor heap is split into a unified region (spark.memory.fraction, ~60%) and user memory (~40%). the unified region is dynamically shared between execution memory (shuffles, joins, sorts) and storage memory (cached data). spark.memory.storagefraction (~50% of unified) sets the protected baseline below which storage is safe from eviction. execution can evict borrowed storage blocks when it needs space; storage cannot evict active execution memory. over-caching steals memory from execution, causing spills; the symptom is slow shuffles, not a cache error. this unified model replaced the old static split where idle memory in one pool could not help the other.

kp: first determine whether the oom is on the driver or an executor, because the causes and fixes differ. driver oom is usually from collect(), topandas(), or assembling a large broadcast; fix by writing to storage instead. executor oom is diagnosed via the spark ui: stages tab (task duration spread), executors tab (gc time), storage tab (cache size), sql tab (plan). data skew is the most common executor oom cause: one task's partition is far larger than the rest. other causes include excessive shuffle, too few partitions, oversized broadcast, and over-caching stealing execution memory. the senior approach is to classify the cause from ui evidence and apply the matching fix, not blindly add memory.

kp: spill-to-disk writes overflow shuffle/sort/aggregation data to local disk when execution memory is exceeded. it prevents oom crashes and keeps the job correct, but disk i/o is orders of magnitude slower than memory. the spark ui reports spill per task as 'spill (memory)' and 'spill (disk)' in the stages tab. uniform spill across all tasks indicates too few partitions or too little memory; concentrated spill on one task indicates data skew. fixes include increasing shuffle partitions, unpersisting unneeded caches, more executor memory, and kryo serialization. the goal is not zero spill but bounded spill; forcing everything into memory risks oom.

kp: csv inference with inferschema=true reads the data twice: once to deduce types, once to load; without it, all columns default to string. json inference inspects a configurable sample of records and merges fields into a superset schema, which can miss fields or infer types too narrowly. parquet and orc store the complete schema in the file footer, so no inference is needed and types are exact. an explicit schema in production eliminates the double-read for csv, removes sampling risk for json, and prevents schema drift. an explicit schema also acts as a data contract: unexpected source changes surface as visible failures at read time. pair an explicit schema with failfast read mode and a corrupt-record column for production-grade error handling.

kp: the small-files problem is when a dataset is stored as too many tiny files, causing metadata overhead, slow file listing, and task scheduling overhead. common causes are streaming writes (few records per micro-batch), high-cardinality partitionby, and over-partitioned batch jobs. metadata overhead grows with file count; on s3, listing millions of files can take minutes before any data is read. spark creates one task per file for reads, so millions of tiny files means millions of tasks with overhead dwarfing the work. write-time fixes include coalesce before write, repartition by partition column, and maxrecordsperfile. post-write fixes include periodic compaction jobs, delta lake optimize, and iceberg/hudi compaction. the ideal file size is 128 mb to 1 gb, aligned with block and row-group sizes.

kp: serialization converts in-memory objects to bytes for transfer between jvms or writing to disk; it is pervasive in spark. all shuffle data, broadcast variables, task closures, and serialized cache data go through the serializer. java serialization is the default: works with any serializable class but is slow and produces large byte streams. kryo serialization is faster and several times more compact, enabled with spark.serializer=kryoserializer. registering classes with kryo lets it write a small integer id instead of the full class name, giving the best size. in the dataframe world, tungsten binary encoders handle most heavy data; the serializer choice matters most for rdd operations and closures. enable kryo by default, register domain classes, and raise the buffer max for large objects.

kp: groupbykey shuffles all raw values for each key to one partition, then lets you aggregate the collected values. reducebykey pre-aggregates values locally on each partition using an associative reduce function before the shuffle. reducebykey shuffles only partial results per key per partition, which can be orders of magnitude less data. groupbykey creates memory pressure on hot keys because all values for a key pile into one partition. in the dataframe api, groupby with sum/count already does map-side pre-aggregation automatically. groupbykey is needed only when you genuinely require the full collection of values per key (like collect_list). the common anti-pattern is groupbykey followed by mapvalues to sum, which shuffles everything when reducebykey would shuffle almost nothing.

kp: distinct() removes rows where all columns match, deduplicating on the entire row. dropduplicates(subset) removes rows where only the specified columns match, keeping one row per distinct key combination. called with no arguments, dropduplicates() behaves identically to distinct(). in banking, the business key is almost always a subset (transaction id), not the whole row, so dropduplicates(subset) is usually correct. dropduplicates keeps an arbitrary surviving row, not necessarily the latest; use a window function with row_number for deterministic selection. both are wide operations requiring a shuffle, so the choice is about correctness, not speed. in structured streaming, dropduplicates is stateful and should be paired with a watermark to bound remembered-keys state.

t: Spark SQL window functions
k: window functions compute per-row values partition order ranking lead running sums moving averages unlike groupby annotate instead collapsing groups summary function computes based related rows defined clause without specifies divide within group optionally frame bounding contribute row_number unique sequence rank ties gaps dense_rank offset read preceding following aggregate windows count ordered produce totals difference collapses single keeps original annotates national bank india imagine statement listing transaction account replacing whole line showing total lose individual transactions keeping adding extra columns beside
kp: window functions compute a value for each row based on a window of related rows defined by an over clause, without collapsing rows. partition by divides rows into groups, order by orders within each group, and an optional frame bounds which rows contribute. row_number gives a unique increasing number per row, rank ties with gaps, and dense_rank ties without gaps. lag reads a value from a preceding row and lead from a following row, enabling period-over-period comparisons without self-joins. sum and avg over an ordered window produce running totals and moving averages while keeping every original row. the key difference from groupby is that groupby collapses each group to one summary row, while a window annotates every row. window functions require a shuffle to gather each partition and a sort to order it, so a skewed partition key causes the same skew problems as a join.

kp: spark security requires four layers working together: authentication, authorization, encryption, and network isolation. authentication uses kerberos in hadoop environments or iam/oauth in cloud, plus spark.authenticate for internal rpc. authorization is enforced through apache ranger, hive table acls, or storage-level permissions for fine-grained access control. encryption at rest uses hdfs transparent encryption or s3 server-side encryption; in transit uses ssl/tls for rpc and spark.network.crypto for shuffle. network isolation places the cluster in private subnets with security groups and firewalls, restricting access to necessary ports only. spark.io.encryption.enabled encrypts intermediate data spilled to local disk by executors. these layers are complementary: authentication without authorization lets any valid user read everything, and strong acls are undermined by an exposed unauthenticated port.

kp: non-deterministic functions return different results across invocations even for the same input because they depend on randomness, state, or partitioning. examples include rand, randn, uuid, monotonically_increasing_id, shuffle, input_file_name, spark_partition_id, and order-sensitive collect_list. catalyst marks them non-deterministic and will not push them below filters or freely reorder them. referencing a dataframe with a non-deterministic column twice without caching can produce different values on each reference. monotonically_increasing_id is not a stable key and should not be used as a reproducible identifier across runs or joins. cache or write-then-read to freeze non-deterministic values so they are computed once and reused consistently. seed rand(seed) for repeatability within a single run, and use sort_array after collect_list when order matters.

kp: permissive is the default mode: keeps bad rows with nulls for unparseable fields and saves the raw bad record in a _corrupt_record column if defined in the schema. dropmalformed silently drops any row that does not conform to the schema, returning only clean rows with no error. failfast throws an exception on the very first malformed record, aborting the entire read immediately. use permissive for bronze layer ingestion where you want to preserve everything and quarantine problems for review. use failfast for strict regulatory feeds where a single bad record signals an upstream problem that must be fixed. the _corrupt_record column must be explicitly added to the schema as a stringtype to capture the raw bad text. dropmalformed is dangerous because it silently loses data; always monitor the drop rate if you use it.

kp: hashaggregate uses an off-heap hash map with mutable fixed-length buffers; it is the fastest and default for sum, count, avg, min, max. sortaggregate sorts by grouping key first, then aggregates runs of equal keys; used when buffers are not mutable fixed-length. objecthashaggregate handles aggregates with arbitrary jvm object buffers like collect_list and collect_set. spark's planner chooses automatically based on whether the aggregate buffers support the mutable fixed-length hash path. you can see which strategy was chosen in the physical plan via explain(). reducing cardinality and avoiding unnecessary collect_list keeps aggregation on the fast hashaggregate path.

kp: a skipped stage is one whose output spark already has from a prior computation, so the dag scheduler reused it instead of re-running its tasks. the most common cause is shuffle output from an earlier job still present on disk, which spark detects and reuses. caching or persisting a dataframe causes downstream stages to be skipped on subsequent actions because the cached blocks serve the data. checkpointing saves results and truncates lineage, so downstream jobs reuse the checkpointed data and skip earlier stages. successive actions on the same cached dataframe show the shared earlier stages as skipped on the second and subsequent jobs. skipped stages are a good sign: they mean spark avoided redundant work and saved computation time. if you expected skipping but see full recomputation, check whether the cache was evicted, the dataframe was not actually cached, or the two actions do not share the stage.

kp: py4j is a library that lets python dynamically call java objects in a jvm over a local socket, making pyspark a thin wrapper over the jvm spark engine. built-in dataframe functions are fast because the entire computation stays inside the jvm; only the small plan description crosses the py4j bridge. plain python udfs are slow because each row is serialized from jvm to a python worker process and back, creating per-row round-trip overhead. pandas (vectorized) udfs use apache arrow to move whole batches in columnar format, cutting the crossing cost by ten to a hundred times. the performance hierarchy is: built-in functions (fastest), pandas udfs (middle), plain python udfs (slowest). the py4j bridge is only on the driver; the per-row udf overhead is on executors between the jvm worker and a separate python worker process. express logic with built-in functions whenever possible; use pandas udfs only when python libraries are truly required; treat plain python udfs as a last resort.

kp: spark's sort() and orderby() are not stable: rows with equal sort keys may appear in any relative order. the instability comes from distributed sorting: data is partitioned across executors, and merge order varies. two runs of the same job can place tied rows in different relative orders. to get deterministic ordering, add a unique tie-breaker column to the sort key. monotonically_increasing_id() provides determinism but not original source order. window functions like row_number() suffer the same tie problem and also need a unique column in the order by.

k: cogroup bundles values rdds separate iterables giving sides together without multiplication join causes transformation takes key-value groups returns iterable cartesian explosion unlike produces matching pair gives full side full-outer behavior exists empty shuffle required partitioned land partition built spark implements internally plus flat imagine national bank india keeps ledgers customer deposits withdrawals deposit withdrawal producing rows really want hand whole list basket another reconcile avoids multiple differ output multiplies collections avoiding useful right tool need custom per-key logic rather pairwise
kp: cogroup groups two key-value rdds by key and returns (key, iterable[v1], iterable[v2]) for each key. unlike a join which produces one output row per matching pair (cartesian explosion), cogroup gives both full groups side by side. if a key exists on only one side, the other iterable is empty, giving natural full-outer behavior. cogroup triggers a shuffle to co-locate values from both rdds by key on the same partition. spark implements join internally on top of cogroup followed by a flat map that produces pairwise combinations. a heavily skewed key with millions of values causes memory pressure, same as groupbykey. in the dataframe world, the same intent is expressed with full outer join plus collect_list, or the structured cogroupeddataset api.

kp: snappy is fast, splittable, and the default for parquet output – the everyday workhorse codec. zstd gives a better compression ratio than snappy with competitive speed and is the modern recommended choice for cold data. gzip gives a good ratio but is slow and not splittable for text files, destroying parallelism on large single files. lz4 is extremely fast with a modest ratio, ideal for hot internal paths like shuffle data. output-format compression (per writer) and internal engine compression (spark.io.compression.codec) are two separate settings. internal compression covers shuffle files, broadcast variables, cached rdd blocks, checkpoint data, and event logs. splittability matters enormously: a single huge gzip csv cannot be parallelized, but snappy or zstd parquet splits at row-group level.

kp: union() matches columns by position: column 1 of df1 is combined with column 1 of df2, regardless of names. unionbyname() matches columns by name: lines up columns correctly even if the order differs between dataframes. union() silently corrupts data if column orders differ, which is one of the nastiest silent bugs in spark. unionbyname with allowmissingcolumns=true (spark 3.1+) fills missing columns with null instead of failing. always prefer unionbyname because names are stable identifiers while positions are fragile. unionbyname still requires compatible types for matched columns, which is desirable as a safety check.

kp: barrier execution mode launches all tasks of a stage together or not at all (gang scheduling), and restarts the entire stage on any single task failure. it is modeled after mpi where all workers must be alive simultaneously for collective communication like all-reduce. the primary use case is distributed deep learning training with frameworks like tensorflow, pytorch, and horovod on spark. you enter barrier mode by calling rdd.barrier().mappartitions(func), which marks the stage as a barrier stage. each task gets a barriertaskcontext with a barrier() synchronization point and gettaskinfos() for peer discovery. you cannot have more barrier tasks than the cluster has concurrent slots, or the stage will never start. barrier mode should never be used for ordinary data processing because it replaces spark's efficient fine-grained fault tolerance with coarse whole-stage retries.

k: catalyst turns dataframe query efficient plan parse analyze optimize physical planning cutting read predicate pushdown column pruning speeding execution whole-stage generation optimizer core spark engine parsed logical parses your text chain tree operators unresolved names analyzed resolves table against catalog checks types optimized rule-based rewrites reduce must generates candidate plans picks cheapest cost model applies fuse compiled bytecode queries expressed declaratively sees entire optimizes dataframes consistently outperform hand-written imagine clerk national bank india receives sloppy request bring transaction record whole
kp: catalyst is spark sql's extensible query optimizer that transforms a dataframe or sql query into an efficient execution plan through four phases. the four phases are: parse, analyze, optimize (rule-based), and physical planning with cost-based strategy selection. predicate pushdown moves filters to the data source so less data is read from parquet or jdbc. column pruning drops columns the query never uses, reducing i/o on columnar formats like parquet. whole-stage code generation fuses a chain of operators into a single compiled java function for tight jvm loops. dataframes and sql outperform hand-written rdd code because catalyst sees the whole query and applies automatic optimizations. catalyst is complemented at runtime by adaptive query execution, which adjusts the physical plan using real statistics.

kp: aqe re-optimizes the physical plan during execution using real runtime statistics gathered at shuffle boundaries. it coalesces many small post-shuffle partitions into fewer, better-sized ones to reduce task overhead. it detects skewed shuffle partitions and splits them so a hot key does not create a straggler task. it dynamically switches join strategies, converting a planned sort-merge join to a broadcast join when a side is small enough. aqe complements catalyst: catalyst plans from estimates up front, aqe corrects the plan with real counts at runtime. aqe is enabled by default in modern spark and works at shuffle boundaries where statistics are naturally available.

kp: window functions compute across related rows without collapsing them, unlike group by which squashes rows into one group. lag reads a value from a previous row in partition order, enabling month-over-month comparisons by looking back one or two periods. row_number numbers rows within a partition so the first occurrence is row 1 and any row above 1 is a suspected duplicate. the over clause defines partition by (grouping), order by (row ordering), and an optional frame (surrounding rows). handle the first month's null from lag with coalesce, and choose the order by inside row_number deliberately to control which copy is the original. both patterns have real financial impact in banking: duplicate detection prevents double-charges, and growth analytics drive relationship management.

k: structured streaming treats live stream unbounded table processed incrementally catalyst-optimized dataframe event-time support exactly-once guarantees replacing legacy rdd-based dstream model incoming record appended never closes your query runs rows micro-batch write groupby filter join select dataframes spark turns incremental computations catalyst optimization goes predicate pushdown column pruning whole-stage generation unlike raw-rdd path watermarks first-class withwatermark window functions late out-of-order events land correct bucket end-to-end checkpointed offsets plus idempotent transactional sinks guarantee reflected exactly once output replacement dstreams were batch-of-rdds at-least-once
kp: structured streaming models a live stream as an unbounded table processed incrementally in micro-batches using the dataframe and sql api. every streaming query is optimized by catalyst with predicate pushdown, column pruning, and whole-stage code generation. event-time processing with watermarks ensures late and out-of-order events land in the correct time window. exactly-once delivery is achieved through checkpointed offsets on the source side and idempotent or transactional sinks on the write side. dstreams were rdd-based, had no catalyst optimization, no event-time support, and could only reach at-least-once delivery. the unbounded table model means you write the same code for streaming as for batch, and spark handles incremental execution automatically.

kp: append mode emits only new, final rows that will never change, and is the only mode supported by file sinks. complete mode rewrites the entire result table every trigger and is valid only for aggregation queries with bounded group counts. update mode emits only changed rows and is the efficient choice for running aggregations to upsert-capable sinks. append mode with aggregation requires a watermark so spark knows when a window is finalized. complete mode never drops state because the full result must remain re-emittable, making it unsuitable for millions of groups. spark rejects invalid query-mode pairings at query start with an analysisexception, failing fast rather than producing wrong output.

kp: a watermark is computed as the maximum event time observed minus a configured delay, and it only advances forward. events with an event time older than the current watermark are dropped as too late for aggregation. state for windows that fully close below the watermark is evicted, which bounds memory in long-running stateful queries. the watermark must be declared on the same event-time column used in the window function to be effective. in append mode with aggregation, the watermark determines when a window result is finalized and emitted. the watermark delay is a correctness-versus-resource trade-off: larger delays capture more late events but increase state size and latency.

kp: stateless operations (filter, select, map) process each micro-batch independently with no memory of previous batches. stateful operations (groupby, join, dropduplicates) maintain a keyed state store across batches and need watermarks to bound memory. stateless queries recover cheaply by replaying from committed offsets; stateful queries must also restore the state store from the checkpoint. changing stateful query logic can make an existing checkpoint incompatible, forcing a state reset. the rocksdb state store handles large state by keeping it off-heap on local disk, avoiding jvm garbage-collection pressure. good streaming design pre-filters statelessly before stateful aggregations to minimize the state footprint.

kp: tumbling windows are fixed-size and non-overlapping; each event belongs to exactly one window. sliding windows overlap by a slide interval, giving more frequent views at the cost of duplicate processing per event. session windows close after a configurable gap of inactivity, grouping bursts of activity dynamically. a watermark is computed as max-event-time minus out-of-orderness tolerance and drives window firing. late events arriving after the watermark has passed their window are dropped by default, but allowed lateness and side outputs can capture them. every window has three components: the assigner (routes events to windows), the trigger (decides when to fire), and the optional evictor (prunes elements).

kp: eager watermarks use small out-of-orderness delays for fast window firing but may drop slightly-delayed events. relaxed watermarks use larger delays to capture almost all late events at the cost of increased latency and memory. the watermark delay is a global latency tax: it affects every window, even those with complete data. the hybrid approach combines an eager watermark with allowed lateness and side outputs for speculative speed plus eventual accuracy. alerts and fraud detection lean eager; settlements and regulatory reports lean relaxed. never guess the delay: measure the real lateness distribution and set the bound to cover the bulk of it.

kp: flink is an open-source distributed stream-processing engine that processes each event as it arrives with sub-second latency. it distinguishes event time from processing time and uses watermarks to handle out-of-order and late data correctly. keyed state is first-class and backed by configurable state backends such as hashmapstatebackend or rocksdb for large state. distributed checkpointing with lightweight barriers gives exactly-once state consistency and, with transactional sinks, end-to-end exactly-once. flink treats batch as a special case of streaming over a bounded dataset so one api serves both. the datastream api gives low-level control while the table api and flink sql provide declarative relational queries with optimizer support. flink is the engine of choice for real-time fraud scoring, live risk limits, and instant settlement signals where correctness and latency both matter.

kp: parallelism is the number of parallel subtasks an operator is split into, and each subtask needs exactly one task slot to execute. a task slot is a unit of execution resource on a taskmanager representing a reserved share of its managed memory. the maximum parallelism a job can run is capped by the total number of slots across all taskmanagers in the cluster. slot sharing lets subtasks from different operators share one slot, so a pipeline needs only as many slots as its highest operator parallelism. default slot sharing groups all operators together, which improves resource utilization and load balance by mixing heavy and light operators. you can isolate resource-hungry operators into separate slot sharing groups so they get dedicated slots. operator chaining fuses consecutive forwarding operators into a single task thread within a slot, eliminating serialization overhead.

kp: the datastream api is a low-level, imperative interface where you process events one at a time with full control over keyed state, timers, and custom operator logic. the table api and flink sql are high-level, declarative interfaces where you write relational queries and flink's optimizer plans and executes them automatically. flink sql unifies batch and streaming so the same query runs over a bounded table as batch or an unbounded stream as a continuous query. the two apis are fully interoperable: you can convert between datastream and table within a single job. use the table api or sql as the default for conciseness and optimizer benefits, and drop to datastream only for custom state machines, timers, or patterns. flink cep is a pattern-matching library built on the datastream api for complex event processing.

kp: session mode runs one long-lived cluster that many jobs submit to and share, ideal for development and interactive exploration. per-job mode spins up a dedicated cluster per job but runs main() on the client, is yarn-only, and is now deprecated. application mode gives each application its own cluster and runs main() on the cluster itself, which is the preferred mode for production. application mode eliminates the client-side bottleneck because the expensive jobgraph construction happens on the cluster. on kubernetes, native application mode lets flink request its own pods as a self-contained, gitops-friendly unit. the practical rule is session mode for development, application mode for production, and avoid per-job mode.

kp: event time is the timestamp embedded in each record describing when the event actually occurred at its source. processing time is the wall-clock time of the machine running the operator at the moment it handles the record. ingestion time is the timestamp assigned by the flink source operator when the record first enters the pipeline. event time gives deterministic, replayable, out-of-order-tolerant results through watermarks but needs more configuration. processing time gives the lowest latency and simplest setup but is non-deterministic and unsuitable for auditable results. event time is the correct default for any financial or audit workload where the business cares about when money moved.

kp: a late event is a record whose event-time timestamp falls into a window that has already fired because the watermark has moved past that window's end. by default flink silently drops late events, which is efficient but loses data without any error. allowed lateness keeps the window state open for a grace period, re-firing the window function on each late arrival to emit corrected results. side outputs capture events that arrive later than the allowed-lateness period, routing them to a separate stream for reconciliation. downstream sinks must be idempotent or upsert-capable because allowed lateness causes re-emissions of window results. the combination of a modest allowed lateness for common stragglers and a side output for rare extreme latecomers gives both low latency and no data loss.

kp: a forwarding edge is a one-to-one connection where each upstream subtask sends records directly to one downstream subtask with no network shuffle. forwarding preserves record order within a partition and allows flink to chain operators into a single task thread with zero serialization overhead. a redistributing edge repartitions records across all downstream subtasks according to a rule like key hashing, requiring serialization and network transfer. keyby hashes each record's key to route it to the correct subtask; rebalance round-robins; broadcast sends to all; rescale redistributes locally. every redistribution is a shuffle boundary that costs cpu for serialization, network bandwidth, and potential backpressure. the performance rule is to minimize shuffles, push filtering and projection before keyby, and watch for key skew that overloads one subtask.

kp: internal exactly-once is guaranteed by barrier-based checkpointing that snapshots operator state and source offsets consistently. end-to-end exactly-once extends this to external sinks by tying the sink's transaction lifecycle to the checkpoint lifecycle. the two-phase commit protocol has four hooks: begintransaction, precommit, commit, and abort, mapped to checkpoint events. the sink pre-commits output when the checkpoint barrier arrives but only commits when the jobmanager confirms the checkpoint is globally complete. kafka sinks use kafka transactions so pre-committed records are invisible to read-committed consumers until commit. the checkpoint interval becomes the end-to-end latency floor for exactly-once output because downstream readers only see data after commit. if the external system cannot do transactions, you can achieve effectively-once with idempotent writes keyed by a deterministic id.

kp: backpressure is flink's automatic flow-control mechanism where a slow downstream operator causes upstream operators and the source to slow down. it works through credit-based flow control: each receiver advertises free buffer credits to senders, and senders can only transmit when credits are available. no records are ever dropped and no special configuration is required; the system self-regulates to the speed of its slowest stage. backpressure is a symptom, not a cause: the real job is to find and fix the slow operator using the web ui and metrics. common bottleneck causes include a slow external sink, heavy computation, data skew overloading one subtask, or insufficient parallelism. backpressure interacts with aligned checkpointing by slowing barrier propagation, which is why unaligned checkpoints exist.

kp: fixed-delay restarts the job a fixed number of times with a constant delay between attempts. failure-rate allows restarts as long as the failure count within a sliding interval stays below a threshold. exponential-delay increases the backoff after each failure up to a maximum, ideal for overloaded dependencies. no-restart fails the job immediately on the first failure, suitable for batch jobs or external orchestrators. with checkpointing enabled, a restart restores from the last checkpoint, so it is a recovery, not a data-loss event. you configure strategies per job via the restartstrategies api or globally in flink-conf.yaml. always monitor restart counts because a job that silently restarts every minute is as broken as one that is down.

kp: the failover strategy decides how much of the job graph to restart, while the restart strategy decides how often. region failover restarts only the failed pipelined region and its dependents, leaving unrelated regions running. a pipelined region is a set of tasks connected by streaming data exchanges, bounded by blocking exchanges. region failover has been the default since flink 1.9 because it minimizes the blast radius of a single failure. full restart cancels every task in the entire job, which is simple but wasteful for multi-pipeline jobs. batch and hybrid jobs benefit most from region failover because blocking exchanges create smaller regions. region failover depends on checkpointing so the restarted region can restore state consistently.

kp: consumer lag is the gap between the latest produced offset and the committed offset, representing unprocessed backlog. steadily growing lag means the consumer cannot keep up and the pipeline is falling behind. partition rebalancing redistributes partitions when a consumer joins, leaves, or dies, causing a brief processing pause. back-pressure propagates slowness upstream so the pipeline runs at the speed of its slowest stage instead of crashing. you scale consumers horizontally up to the partition count, which sets maximum parallelism. poison records are retried a bounded number of times, then routed to a dead-letter queue so they never block the partition. cooperative incremental rebalancing reduces pause duration compared to the older stop-the-world rebalance.

kp: merge into is a single atomic upsert that matches source to target on a key and applies update, delete, and insert in one transaction. it is atomic and isolated: concurrent readers always see a consistent snapshot, never a half-applied batch. the manual read-check-write pattern races with concurrent writers and can lose updates or create duplicates. merge rewrites only the files that contain matched rows, not the entire table. the source must never match a target row more than once; delta rejects ambiguous matches to keep results deterministic. use partition or zorder predicates to narrow the match condition so merge touches fewer files.

kp: optimize compacts many small data files into fewer larger ones to improve read performance; it does not change the data. zorder by co-locates related data within files so delta's min/max statistics can skip files on filtered queries. vacuum permanently deletes old unreferenced data files beyond the retention period to reclaim storage. vacuuming below the retention window breaks time travel because it destroys the files that historical versions relied on. storage temporarily grows after optimize because old files linger until vacuum removes them past the retention period. the healthy pattern is: optimize regularly for read speed, vacuum periodically for storage, and set retention to match audit requirements.

kp: data skew produces one giant partition after a shuffle, creating a straggler task that holds up the entire stage. aqe detects skew using two thresholds: partition size must exceed skewedpartitionfactor times the median and exceed skewedpartitionthresholdinbytes. aqe splits the skewed partition into sub-partitions and replicates the other join side so each sub-partition joins independently. manual salting is needed when a single key is so dominant that even split sub-partitions are too large. aqe's skew handling targets joins specifically; heavily skewed aggregations or window operations still need salting or pre-aggregation. salting appends a random suffix to the key on the fact side and expands the dimension side to match, spreading the hot key evenly.

kp: bucketing spreads rows across a fixed number of files by hashing a column, enabling shuffle-free joins and aggregations on that column. the bucketing column must be high cardinality and aligned with join or group keys for even distribution. bucket count should match cluster parallelism, roughly one bucket per core, with each bucket sized in the hundreds of megabytes. bucketing metadata lives only in the metastore: you must write with saveastable and read through the catalog table. both sides of a bucket-aware join must share the identical bucket count and column, or spark re-shuffles. delta lake does not support classic hive-style bucketing; use optimize and zorder or liquid clustering instead.

t: Why min/max and dictionary filtering fail on high-cardinality unsorted columns, and how bloom filters help

kp: min/max statistics fail on high-cardinality unsorted columns because every block's range spans the entire domain, so no block can be skipped. dictionary filtering fails because high cardinality means the dictionary is too large or parquet drops dictionary encoding entirely. bloom filters store a compact bitset per block; testing a value gives 'definitely not present' (safe skip) or 'probably present' (must read). bloom filters never produce false negatives, which makes skipping safe, and they are compact regardless of value count. enable bloom filters per column at write time only for high-cardinality equality lookups like transaction_id or customer_id. bloom filters help equality and in predicates only, not range queries, because hashing destroys order.

kp: do not broadcast when the small side does not fit in executor memory after deserialization: it causes oom, which is worse than a slow sort-merge join. do not broadcast when both sides are large: neither qualifies, and a sort-merge join is the safe choice. deserialized in-memory size can be several times the on-disk size, so a table that looks small on disk can still oom. the rule 'smaller does not mean safe to broadcast' captures that broadcasting cares about absolute size, not relative size. raising the autobroadcastjointhreshold globally is dangerous because it tells spark to broadcast larger sizes across every join. account for executor memory configuration and concurrent tasks: many tasks each holding a broadcast copy multiply the footprint.

kp: a broadcast variable is a low-level spark primitive that distributes any read-only object to executors once, used for map-side lookups. a broadcast join is a high-level sql/dataframe join optimization that broadcasts a small table to avoid shuffling the large side. use broadcast variables for non-relational lookups in rdd code, udfs, or distributing non-tabular objects like models. use broadcast joins for relational joins of dataframes or sql tables where one side is small enough. in modern dataframe-centric spark, most enrichment is better expressed as a join that becomes a broadcast join. both carry the same memory caution: the broadcast object must fit comfortably in executor memory.

kp: isolate-and-broadcast removes hot keys from the shuffle path by joining them separately with a broadcast join. increasing shuffle parallelism helps when many moderately-hot keys collide but does not fix a single mega-key. pre-aggregation at the map side reduces data volume on the hot key before it crosses the shuffle boundary. switching to a broadcast hash join avoids shuffling the large skewed side entirely when the small side fits in memory. redesigning the data model by splitting a hot key into sub-keys is the most durable fix but the most expensive to implement. in production you usually combine two or three techniques and pick based on the specific symptom. always start with the cheapest and most surgical technique that fits the symptom before escalating.

kp: always start by reading the execution plan to find where time is spent before choosing an optimization. date or range partitioning lets the engine prune whole partitions so a date-range query skips irrelevant months. a composite index chosen from the where clause and a covering index that includes select columns enables index-only scans. a materialized view or pre-aggregation table serves repeated rollups from a tiny summary instead of rescanning billions of rows. query rewrites such as replacing correlated subqueries with joins, pushing filters early, and avoiding functions on indexed columns remove avoidable work. in columnar warehouses, partition pruning and predicate pushdown are the storage-level equivalents of these techniques. each optimization must be justified by comparing the execution plan before and after the change.

kp: a narrow dependency means each parent partition feeds at most one child partition, enabling pipelining with no shuffle. a wide dependency means one parent partition feeds multiple children, forcing an expensive network shuffle and a stage boundary. consecutive narrow operations are grouped into one stage; each wide dependency starts a new stage. reducebykey is preferred over groupbykey because it combines locally before the shuffle, sending far less data. co-partitioned or bucketed datasets can turn a join from a wide dependency into a narrow one by pre-locating matching keys. data skew on a wide dependency creates straggler tasks because one shuffle partition becomes much larger than the rest.

kp: spark records a dag of transformations (lineage) for every rdd instead of replicating data for fault tolerance. when an executor fails, the driver recomputes only the lost partitions by replaying their lineage, not the entire job. recomputation is correct because rdds are immutable and transformations are deterministic. narrow dependencies make recovery cheap (one parent partition); wide dependencies are costlier (many parents plus a shuffle). checkpointing truncates long lineage chains by writing an rdd to reliable storage so recovery starts from the checkpoint. caching is a performance optimization, not durability; a lost cached partition is silently recomputed from lineage.

kp: caching everything fills executor storage and forces eviction, often making jobs slower than no caching at all. cache() is lazy; it marks the dataset but materializes only when an action triggers computation. caching data used only once wastes memory for no reuse benefit. forgetting unpersist() in long-running applications accumulates dead caches until storage is exhausted. collect() pulls all data to the driver and can crash it; cache() keeps partitions distributed on executors. caching does not eliminate a shuffle; it only avoids recomputing the lineage (including the shuffle) on subsequent actions.

kp: projection pushdown reads only the columns the query actually needs, skipping the rest at the storage level. in columnar formats like parquet and orc, each column is stored separately, so reading 5 of 100 columns reads about 5% of the data. catalyst determines the needed columns by analyzing the entire logical plan, not just the final select. even if an early step selects many columns, pruning is based on what survives to the final output, filters, joins, and aggregations. row-based formats like csv and json cannot truly prune columns because fields are interleaved on each line. projection pushdown and predicate pushdown work together: one skips columns, the other skips rows.

kp: explode() produces one row per array element and drops rows where the array is null or empty. explode_outer() keeps rows with null or empty arrays, emitting a single row with null in the exploded column. explode behaves like an inner join with the array; explode_outer behaves like a left-outer join. filter and select before exploding because every surviving parent row and every carried column is duplicated per element. posexplode and posexplode_outer additionally emit the element's position index. when the parent has multiple arrays, exploding each separately can create a cross-product; use arrays_zip or higher-order functions instead.

t: The 4 Steps of a System Design Interview
k: clarify sketch boxes deep-dive risky parts talk trade-offs never jump straight solution design interview structured conversation interviewer gives open-ended problem evaluates decompose scalable reliable architecture step requirements questions separate functional non-functional well down scale high-level draw major components label connections protocols flows deep dive zoom three carry risk complexity load explain work internally scaling openly discuss compromises made name bottlenecks grows under increasing imagine rajesh walks national bank india says want build money transfer service good banker immediately start digging
kp: a system design interview follows four disciplined steps: clarify, sketch, deep-dive, and discuss trade-offs. step 1 separates functional requirements from non-functional requirements and pins down scale with back-of-envelope numbers. step 2 draws the high-level architecture with boxes for services, databases, caches, and queues connected by labelled arrows. step 3 deep-dives into the two or three components that carry the most risk or load, such as the atomic debit-credit in banking. step 4 explicitly names trade-offs like consistency versus availability and bottlenecks like a single primary database. time-boxing is critical: roughly five minutes on requirements, ten on design, fifteen on deep dive, and the rest on trade-offs. the single biggest mistake candidates make is skipping straight to a solution without clarifying scope first.

t: Back-of-Envelope Estimation (QPS, Storage, Bandwidth, Servers)

kp: back-of-envelope estimation turns vague scale requirements into concrete numbers using round figures and simple arithmetic. qps is computed by dividing daily volume by 86,400 seconds and multiplying by a peak factor of 2 to 10. storage is record size multiplied by records per day multiplied by retention period. bandwidth is payload size multiplied by peak request rate, telling you whether you need a cdn or compression. server count is peak qps divided by per-server capacity, plus a buffer for redundancy. always state your assumptions out loud so the interviewer can correct them. the interviewer cares about your reasoning process, not about getting a perfectly precise number.

k: functional non-functional fast reliably correctly requirements concrete behaviours must provide features inputs outputs define testable yes-or-no feature check quality attributes constrain well delivered latency availability consistency durability security scalability service level objective numeric target requirement under tension often conflict designer explicit trade-offs aligned domain national bank india opens teller counter customer withdraw cash withdrawal complete thirty seconds open business hours amount shown always exactly match ledger describes rest describe good right thing slowly sometimes wrong numbers still fails banking transfer
kp: functional requirements describe what the system does : features, inputs, and outputs testable by a yes-or-no check. non-functional requirements describe how well it does it : latency, availability, consistency, durability, security, and scalability. functional requirements map directly to api endpoints and use cases. non-functional requirements are measured against numeric targets and service level objectives. the four most discussed nfrs in interviews are latency (p99), availability (nines), consistency (strong vs eventual), and scalability (peak qps). nfrs usually conflict : strong consistency fights availability during a network partition (cap theorem). for money, favour consistency and durability; for a social feed, favour availability and speed.

t: Design a Distributed Cache (like Redis/Memcached)

kp: a distributed cache is an in-memory key-value store spread across nodes that serves hot data at microsecond latency. consistent hashing distributes keys across nodes so adding or removing a node moves only a small fraction of keys. lru evicts the entry untouched longest (temporal locality); lfu evicts the least accessed (permanent hot keys). write-through updates cache and database together for consistency; write-behind writes cache first and flushes async for speed. ttl-based invalidation is simple but allows brief staleness; event-based invalidation is precise but requires wiring. cache stampede occurs when a hot key expires and many requests miss simultaneously; prevent with single-flight locks. for banking balances, use write-through with event-based invalidation to never serve a stale number.

t: Load Balancer
k: spread traffic across healthy servers algorithm route connection request content never send server failed health check load balancer component distributes incoming network pool backend maximize throughput minimize latency provide fault tolerance layer routes transport-level information address port without reading body extremely fast protocol-agnostic application-level http path cookies headers enables content-based routing periodic probe removes unhealthy backends rotation until recover distribution rule choosing gets next round-robin least-connections hash customers crowd national bank india floor manager stands entrance directs person open teller
kp: a load balancer distributes incoming traffic across a pool of backend servers for throughput, fault tolerance, and latency. layer 4 (transport) forwards by ip and port without reading the request; it is extremely fast and protocol-agnostic. layer 7 (application) reads http path, cookies, or headers, enabling content-based routing to different service pools. round-robin cycles through servers equally; least-connections favours the least busy; ip hash provides session stickiness. health checks periodically probe each backend and remove unhealthy instances from rotation. keep servers stateless and store sessions in a shared cache rather than relying on sticky sessions for better failover. deploy load balancers as highly available pairs so the balancer itself is not a single point of failure.

kp: a cdn is a geographically distributed network of edge servers that cache static content close to users for low-latency delivery. on a cache miss the edge fetches from the origin once, stores it, and serves all subsequent requests until the ttl expires. the cache key (usually the url) decides what counts as the same object; incorrect keys can leak personalized content. versioned urls (logo-v2.png) are preferred over explicit invalidation because purging is slow and costly. only cache content identical for every user; dynamic personalized content must stay off the edge or use per-user cache keys. signed, time-limited urls protect private or premium content so only authorized users can fetch it. cdns also provide ddos absorption and api acceleration by routing through optimized backbone networks.

kp: aws cloudfront is amazon's managed cdn with 400+ global edge locations, integrated with s3, alb, ec2, and lambda@edge. cache behaviors match path patterns to origins with specific ttl, cache-key, and origin-failover settings. origin groups provide automatic failover: if the primary origin fails, cloudfront serves from a secondary. invalidation purges paths from all edges, but versioned object names are preferred for frequent changes. signed urls and cookies restrict access to private content; origin access control locks s3 so only cloudfront can reach it. lambda@edge and cloudfront functions run code at the edge for header injection, url rewriting, and lightweight auth. cloudfront integrates with aws shield for ddos protection and waf for request filtering at the edge.

kp: sql databases provide acid transactions, strong consistency, enforced schemas, and rich relational queries with joins. nosql stores trade some consistency for horizontal scale, flexible schemas, and predictable key-based access at massive volume. in-memory caches like redis provide microsecond reads for hot data but are not the durable source of truth. choose sql when correctness is non-negotiable and data is relational (bank ledger, transfers, reconciliation). choose nosql when you need massive scale with simple key-based access and flexible schema (activity logs, sessions). add a cache in front when data is hot and read often, using cache-aside with invalidation on writes. real systems use polyglot persistence : sql for the ledger, nosql for the activity feed, redis for balances.

t: Consistent Hashing
k: place nodes keys hash ring assign next node clockwise adding removing moves small slice consistent hashing distribution technique maps server onto conceptual function assignment belongs encountered position minimal movement remaps instead nearly modulo virtual physical placed many points smooth balance load replication achieved walking distinct placing copies different machines suppose national bank india stores customer records across several branches taking account number branch count opens closes changes suddenly almost record forcing massive migration smarter scheme picture clock face around assigned
kp: consistent hashing maps both keys and nodes onto a ring and assigns each key to the first node clockwise from it. adding or removing a node remaps only about 1/n of the keys, not nearly all as naive modulo hashing would. virtual nodes give each physical node many ring positions, smoothing out uneven key distribution and load. it is the backbone of distributed caches (memcached), databases (cassandra, dynamodb), and partitioned systems. replication is achieved by walking clockwise to the next n distinct physical nodes from the key's position. weighting virtual node counts lets heterogeneous hardware carry proportional load. the problem it solves is the instability of modulo hashing, where changing the node count reshuffles nearly every key.

t: Database Sharding
k: split rows across database instances shard scale beyond machine pick balance load keep queries single-shard plan painful resharding sharding horizontal partitioning splits dataset multiple holding disjoint subset column determines lives choice governs query efficiency hash-based hashes even distribution loses range locality range-based maps ranges shards scans risks hotspots cross-shard must touch scatter-gather slow complex adding capacity requires moving operationally challenging national bank india many customers ledger book hold several books rule account numbers ending smaller faster search clerks work different
kp: sharding is horizontal partitioning that splits rows across multiple database instances to scale beyond one machine. the shard key is the single most important decision: it governs load balance and query efficiency. a good shard key spreads data evenly and keeps common queries on a single shard (e.g., account id for banking). hash-based sharding spreads load evenly but loses range locality; range-based allows range scans but risks hotspots. cross-shard queries (scatter-gather) and cross-shard transactions are expensive and must be minimized by design. resharding with naive modulo remaps nearly all rows; use virtual shards or consistent hashing for minimal disruption. plan the shard key before you need it, because retrofitting onto a live system is one of the riskiest migrations.
