k: copy replicas read scale availability master-slave writer master-master many writers needing conflict resolution failover promotes replica primary dies replication copying database others improve scalability durability primary-replica single accepts writes replicates read-only serve reads multiple nodes accept must resolve conflicts concurrent touch delay write appears promoting fails requiring detection promotion fencing national bank india keeps official master ledger changes written several photocopies tellers across branches crowd copies tiny moment destroyed photocopy promoted become instead might record conflicting account need rules reconcile
kp: master-slave replication has one primary for all writes and read-only replicas that scale read-heavy workloads. replication lag is the delay before a write on the primary appears on a replica, causing read-your-own-write anomalies. route a user's read to the primary right after their own write to guarantee they see their change immediately. master-master lets multiple nodes accept writes but introduces conflicts; dangerous for money due to conflicting balance writes. failover promotes the most up-to-date replica to primary and fences off the old primary to prevent split-brain. asynchronous replication risks losing recently acknowledged writes on failover; synchronous replication protects them at higher latency. for banking, resolve the async-vs-sync trade-off toward durability because losing an acknowledged transaction is worse than slower writes.

t: CAP Theorem in Practice
k: network partitions must pick rejects requests stay correct serves stale available systems choose eventual consistency bank money chooses theorem distributed cannot simultaneously guarantee availability partition tolerance during sacrifice read sees recent write request gets non-error response keeps working despite dropped messages nodes preserve correctness possibly tunable choosing trade-off operation rather globally imagine national india branches connected phone line ledgers sync goes dead branch decide either refuse anyone touch account until restored numbers blocks customers transact outdated copy reconcile later open
kp: the cap theorem states that during a network partition, a distributed system must sacrifice either consistency or availability. partition tolerance is not optional in a distributed system because networks genuinely fail. cp systems reject requests during a partition to preserve correctness (banking ledger, inventory counts). ap systems serve possibly stale data during a partition to stay available (social feeds, trending lists). most internet-scale consumer systems choose ap with eventual consistency for maximum availability. cap is a per-operation decision, not a global switch : the same bank can be cp for transfers and ap for feed display. tunable consistency lets you choose the right trade-off per data type within the same system.

t: SQL vs NoSQL: When to Use Which
k: acid relations complex queries nosql scale flexible schema simple key-based access choose correctness needs versus pattern databases relational stores fixed schemas enforced relationships transactions optimized family non-relational document key-value wide-column graph horizontal specific patterns atomicity consistency isolation durability guarantees group changes either commit roll back polyglot persistence transactional core scale-out workloads within newsql offer cockroachdb tidb national bank india keeps official accounts strict ruled ledger column defined entry must balance related records linked database firehose clickstream device logs varying shapes
kp: sql databases have fixed schemas, enforced relationships, acid transactions, and powerful queries with joins and aggregations. nosql databases offer flexible schemas, horizontal scale, and predictable key-based access, typically with tunable consistency. nosql covers four shapes: document (mongodb), key-value (dynamodb/redis), wide-column (cassandra), and graph (neo4j). choose sql when you need acid, relational queries, and stable schemas (bank ledger, reconciliation). choose nosql when you need horizontal scale, flexible schema, and key-based access (activity logs, sessions). modern systems use polyglot persistence : sql for the transactional core, nosql for scale-out workloads. newsql databases (cockroachdb, tidb) blur the line by offering acid at horizontal scale.

t: Synchronous vs Asynchronous Communication
k: sync rest grpc waits immediate answer couples caller callee async kafka hands message decouples trading immediacy resilience synchronous communication sends request blocks waiting response giving results tight coupling asynchronous continues without decoupling eventual rather cascading failure slow dependency ties threads brings down whole chain circuit breaker pattern stops calling failing service threshold returning fallback instead blocking rajesh asks teller balance counter until answers drops loan application leaves department processes later national bank india conversations customer needs right drop-boxes work happen
kp: synchronous (rest/grpc) blocks the caller until it gets a response : simple reasoning, tight coupling, cascading failure risk. asynchronous (kafka/sqs) sends a message and continues : decoupled, buffered, resilient, but results are not immediate. use sync when the caller genuinely needs the result to proceed (balance read, authentication). use async when work can happen in the background, you need to buffer spikes, or one event triggers many reactions. real systems mix both : the sync path does the minimum for the user, everything deferrable goes async. protect sync edges with timeouts, retries, and circuit breakers so a slow dependency cannot cascade. async consumers must be idempotent because delivery is typically at-least-once.

t: Push vs Pull Model
k: pull means client keeps asking polling long-polling push server delivers websocket notifications choose latency frequency direction short requests updates fixed interval simple wastes adds long makes request holds open until update timeout reconnects server-sent events one-way server-to-client single long-lived http connection auto-reconnect full-duplex bidirectional send notification platform-specific delivery apns reaches device even closed rajesh wants know cheque cleared keep phoning national bank india minutes pulling instant clears initiating everyone nothing changed news immediately requires reach simplest trivial build works everywhere
kp: pull means the client keeps asking (polling, long-polling); push means the server delivers on its own (websocket, sse, push notifications). short polling is simple but wastes requests when nothing changed and adds latency up to the polling interval. long polling holds the request open until there is an update or timeout, giving near-real-time delivery over http. sse (server-sent events) streams one-way events over a single long-lived http connection with auto-reconnect. websocket is full-duplex bidirectional communication, ideal for interactive use like chat or live trading. mobile push notifications (apns/fcm) reach a device even when the app is closed, essential for fraud alerts. for millions of mostly idle clients, push notifications or long-polling can be cheaper than holding millions of websockets.

t: Monolith vs Microservices
k: start monolith simplicity speed move microservices scale independent deployment team autonomy outweigh added distributed-system complexity single deployable application modules process share codebase database independently services owning communicating network saga pattern sequence local transactions step compensating action undoes later fails service mesh infrastructure layer istio linkerd handles service-to-service communication retries observability running national bank india building department shares filing room simple small giving staff records connected couriers helps huge must manage many buildings risk courier delayed keeps functionality usually advantages early
kp: a monolith is a single deployable application where all modules share one process and database : simple to build, test, and deploy. microservices decompose the system into independently deployable services, each owning its data and communicating over the network. start with a monolith for simplicity and speed; extract services when a specific scaling or deployment pain appears. microservices enable independent scaling, independent deployment, fault isolation, and team autonomy at scale. the costs are real: no distributed transaction by default, network failures, operational complexity (discovery, logging, tracing). premature microservices on a small team trade simple in-process calls for distributed-system complexity before it is justified. use the saga pattern (compensating actions) instead of distributed transactions across microservices.

t: Build vs Buy
k: build differentiates commodity infrastructure judge total cost ownership opportunity better usually means maintain forever core differentiator something customers choose competitors cannot easily copy worth building fraud model scoring algorithm solved problem many vendors provide equally well buying email blob storage message queue full including initial ongoing maintenance security patches scaling on-call burden vendor lock-in difficulty switching third-party service once deeply integrated sovereignty regulatory requirement keep sensitive within specific jurisdictions restrict choice national bank india must decide whether email-sending provider fraud-scoring
kp: build what differentiates you (proprietary fraud model); buy commodity infrastructure (email, blob storage, message queue). total cost of ownership includes ongoing maintenance, upgrades, security patches, scaling, and on-call burden, not just initial development. vendor lock-in and data-sovereignty risks can push the decision toward building, especially for regulated banking data. time to market heavily favours buying : a bought solution ships weeks faster than a built one. "we can build it better" usually means "we will maintain it forever" : the long tail is the expensive part. the decision is reversible : buy to reach market, then selectively build later if it becomes a differentiator. prefer vendors with open standards to limit lock-in and keep the option to switch.

t: Strong Consistency vs Eventual Consistency
k: strong consistency means read sees latest write money eventual replicas converge delay fine feeds counts returns recent committed observers single up-to-date absence writes reads temporarily stale read-your-writes user always changes immediately even users slightly later causal preserves cause-and-effect ordering related operations tunable choosing operation many must acknowledge cassandra quorum rajesh transfers national bank india moment transfer succeeds teller screen show balance exceptions wrong allow double-spend likes post community feed friend updated count once commits subsequent anywhere newer achieving requires coordination
kp: strong consistency guarantees every read returns the most recent committed write : required for money. eventual consistency guarantees replicas converge after a delay : acceptable for feeds, counts, and analytics. strong consistency requires coordination (single leader, quorum reads) which adds latency and reduces partition availability. eventual consistency allows low-latency, highly available reads from any replica. read-your-writes consistency ensures a user sees their own changes immediately, even if others see them slightly later. tunable consistency (cassandra) lets you choose per operation how many replicas must acknowledge. consistency is a per-data-type decision, not a single global setting for the whole system.

k: batch processes bounded dataset high-throughput pass spark streaming unbounded event flow latency arrives flink kafka streams processing runs large collected period optimized throughput apache dominant engine stream computes results incrementally continuous events common engines windowing grouping intervals tumbling hopping sliding aggregation watermark marker tracks event-time progress knows window finalized checkpointing periodically saving state fault-tolerant recovery without reprocessing everything national bank india gathers transaction compute interest reports done fixed pile overnight fraud team needs catch suspicious within seconds watch live react
kp: batch processing runs a job over a bounded dataset in one high-throughput pass; results are available only after the job completes. stream processing computes incrementally over an unbounded event flow with low latency as data arrives. spark is the dominant batch engine; flink and kafka streams are common stream engines. use batch for historical analysis, end-of-day reports, reconciliation, and regulatory filings. use streaming for fraud detection, real-time dashboards, live alerts, and event-driven reactions. modern architectures run both: streaming for real-time reactions, batch for periodic authoritative recomputation. stream processing must handle event-time vs processing-time, watermarks for late data, and checkpointing for fault tolerance.

kp: a rate limiter controls how many requests a client may make in a time window, rejecting excess with http 429. fixed window counts per calendar interval but has a boundary flaw allowing double the rate at minute edges. sliding window blends current and previous window counts to smooth the boundary problem. token bucket refills at a steady rate up to a capacity, cleanly allowing bursts while enforcing an average. in distributed systems, rate-limit state lives in redis with atomic lua scripts to prevent race conditions. place the limiter at the api gateway so bad traffic is rejected before reaching downstream services. use different rate limits per endpoint: cheap balance reads get higher limits than expensive transfers.

k: csrf rides victim auto-sent cookie stop unguessable token samesite cookies cross-site request forgery attack tricks browser sending unwanted state-changing site already authenticated root cause automatically attaches domain regardless initiated synchronizer secret per-session anti-csrf embedded forms headers attacker cannot read guess attribute strict stops requests affected apis authorization bearer instead browsers auto-attach custom rajesh logged national bank india another visits malicious secretly contains hidden form auto-submits transfer sees seemingly valid instruction obeys requiring one-time stamp genuine pages print know forged rejected
kp: csrf tricks a logged-in user's browser into sending an unwanted, state-changing request to a site where the user is already authenticated. it works because browsers automatically attach cookies to any request to a domain, regardless of which site initiated it. the synchronizer token pattern embeds an unguessable anti-csrf token in forms that the attacker cannot read or guess. the samesite cookie attribute (strict or lax) tells the browser not to attach cookies on cross-site requests. token-based apis with authorization headers are not csrf-prone because browsers do not auto-attach custom headers. spring security enables csrf protection by default for session-based applications.

t: Broken Authentication and Best Practices
tp: Web Vulnerabilities: SQLi, XSS, CSRF, SSRF
k: protect login itself strong hashed passwords lockout rate limiting well-managed tokens broken authentication weaknesses attackers compromise user identity process weak short common stored hashing sha-1 plaintext missing account repeated failures enables brute force credential stuffing without multi-factor stolen password gives full access poor token management predictable session exposed urls rotation invalidation logout username enumeration different error messages timing valid invalid usernames reveals accounts exist national bank india letting anyone guess customer many times want accepting writing pins sticky notes never
kp: broken authentication is a class of weaknesses that let attackers compromise user identity through the login process itself. weak passwords are defended by enforcing minimum length, screening against breached-password lists, and hashing with bcrypt or argon2. brute force and credential stuffing are defended by rate limiting, account lockout after repeated failures, and captcha. multi-factor authentication (mfa) ensures a stolen password alone is not enough for account access. session tokens must be high-entropy, httponly, secure, samesite, rotated on login, and invalidated on logout. respond to login failures with uniform generic messages and timing to prevent username enumeration.

tp: Web Vulnerabilities: SQLi, XSS, CSRF, SSRF

kp: sensitive data exposure is the failure to protect confidential data at rest, in transit, and in logs. passwords must be hashed with slow algorithms (bcrypt, argon2) and never stored recoverable. data in transit must be encrypted with tls: enforce https everywhere and enable hsts. logs must never contain passwords, full card numbers, tokens, or raw pii: mask sensitive fields. recoverable sensitive data (account numbers, pii) should be encrypted at rest or tokenized. encryption key management: rotation and separation of keys from data is as important as the encryption itself.

t: Principle of Least Privilege
tp: Web Vulnerabilities: SQLi, XSS, CSRF, SSRF
k: grant minimum permission needed compromise damage principle least privilege polp user service process credential granted permissions required perform function nothing blast radius limits mistakes bugs compromised accounts confining breached identity multi-layer applies application roles database grants cloud policies file network access just-in-time elevation extra rights duration revoke automatically separation duties single initiate approve sensitive action national bank india teller opens drawer vault cleaner pass lobby server room nobody carries master stolen thief reaches whole handing person machine exactly keys needs
kp: least privilege means every user, service, and credential gets only the minimum permissions needed for its function. it limits blast radius: a compromised identity can only do the small set of things it was explicitly allowed. it applies at every layer: application roles, database grants, cloud iam policies, file permissions, and network access. just-in-time elevation grants extra rights only for the minutes needed, then automatically revokes them. common anti-patterns: wildcard permissions, shared admin accounts, and temporary grants that never get removed. in banking, least privilege is often a regulatory requirement, not just good engineering practice.

t: SSRF (Server-Side Request Forgery) and How to Prevent It
tp: Web Vulnerabilities: SQLi, XSS, CSRF, SSRF
k: ssrf makes your trusted server fetch attacker-chosen urls allowlist destinations block internal metadata addresses server-side request forgery vulnerability attacker supplies crafted fetches making http requests destination choosing access comes reach apis admin panels cloud endpoint primary defense strict permitted hosts schemes resolved validation check reject loopback link-local egress proxy route outbound controlled gateway enforces rules centrally imagine national bank india errand whatever address customer writes slip normally customers write clever safe-room read master list insider pass walks straight room never
kp: ssrf tricks the server into making http requests to attacker-chosen destinations by supplying a crafted url. because the request originates from the trusted server, it can reach internal resources the attacker cannot access directly. the primary defense is a strict allowlist of permitted hosts plus blocking private, loopback, and link-local ip ranges. the defense must check the resolved ip at connection time, not just the textual url, to defeat dns rebinding. the cloud metadata endpoint (169.254.169.254) is the most dangerous target: it can hand out iam credentials. never pass raw user input as a url to an http client; route outbound calls through a controlled egress proxy.
